units.la: ON ita pridem in lucem prodiit Celeberrimi D. Spanhemii Epistola de novissimis circa res sacras in Belgio dissidiis, qua visa atque perlecta Obstupui steteruntque comæ, & vox faucibus hæsit.
units.tr: Not long ago there appeared in print the most celebrated Mr. Spanheim's Letter on the Recent Disputes in Belgium concerning Sacred Matters. On seeing and reading it, I was struck with horror, my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat.

units.la: Stupebam enim in innocentes & nihil tale meritos, omne jactari calumniarum genus, idque eo artificio, eaque calliditate, ut justus, ne incautos & rerum notrarum ignaros seduceret, metus quemlibet bonum incesserit. Ei nihil reponere, nec calumniandi quibus peritissimè utitur artes detegere, tutissimum forte foret. Terrent enim me omninò aliorum vestigia. & abstinerem certè ab hoc proposito, nisi mei officii putarem famam honestorum & pacis amantium virorum quam subdole admodum in illa epistola læsam animadvertebam, quantum in me erat, ab illius Theologi calumniis immunem præstare. Provinciam suscepi, fateor, arduam. Sic jubet ipsa ratio, jubet causæ quam propugno veritas; quæ sola eam in me fiduciam procreat, ut ausim quid de illa Epistola sentiam, palam facere. quod ipsum brevi nec cómpto vel ad ostentationem declamatoriam composito, sed simplici & vulgari sermone expediam.
units.tr: I was astonished that every kind of slander was hurled at innocent men who had deserved nothing of the sort, and with such craft and cunning that, lest he mislead the unwary and those ignorant of our affairs, the just man would strike fear into anyone of goodwill. To answer him and expose the slanders in which he is so skilled would perhaps be the safest course. Indeed, the fate of others terrifies me, and I would certainly refrain from this undertaking, had I not thought it my duty to keep, as far as lay in me, the reputation of honourable men who love peace free from that theologian's slanders, a reputation which I saw had been injured in that letter with great craftiness. I have undertaken, I confess, a difficult task. Reason itself demands it, and the truth of the cause I defend demands it; truth alone gives me the confidence to dare to make public what I think of that Letter. I shall set this out briefly, not polished or composed for show or for declamatory display, but in plain and ordinary speech.

units.la: Postquam populi rumore intellexeramus parari à Cl. Spanhemio fulmen vibrandum in capita sic dictorum Novatorum, arrectis auribus adstitimus attentique ora tenuimus, observaturi quid tantum oraculum esset responsurum, & quibus tonitruis turres disjecturum. verùm postquam expe-cta-
units.tr: After we had learned by public report that Mr. Spanheim was preparing a thunderbolt to hurl at the heads of the so-called Novatores, we stood with ears pricked up and held our breath, intent on seeing what so great an oracle would answer and with what thunders he would bring down their towers. But after we had waited long enough,

units.la: stavimus sic satis, accidit nobis quod illis qui parturientis montis acciti clamoribus convenerant spectatum undique, frustratamque expectationem suam mirabantur: quippe, ut ait Poëta, Mons parturibat gemitus immanes ciens, Eratque in terris maxima exspectatio Quid ille pareret: at ille murem peperit.
units.tr: what happened to us was what happened to those who had gathered from every side at the clamour of a mountain in labour, and who marvelled that their expectation was frustrated. For, as the poet says, "The mountain was in labour, sending forth dreadful groans, and there was the greatest expectation on earth of what it would bring forth; and it brought forth a mouse."

units.la: Neque enim Cl. Spanhemius extricabat illa quæ minabatur, quique expectabamus & eruditam & modestam paginam, nihil tale impetravimus, sed flosculos vocum, sed verborum mare, rerum autem, ut dicebat ille, guttas;
units.tr: For Mr. Spanheim did not deliver what he threatened. We who expected a learned and moderate page got nothing of the kind, but only little flowers of words, a sea of verbiage, and, as the saying goes, mere drops of matter.

units.la: Proiicit ampullas & scsquipedalia verba.
units.tr: "He throws away his bombast and words a foot and a half long."

units.tr: For the rest, if not in all things at least as far as the main and principal part is concerned, his account is

units.la: Pergula pictoris, veri nihil, omnia ficta. Oratoriam. tamen ejus, & undique sparsos flores, quis non miretur? cogitabam Quam lepidè lexeis compostæ! ut tesserulæ omnes Arte, pavimento, atque emblemate vermiculato!
units.tr: "a painter's backdrop, nothing true, everything made up." Yet who would not marvel at his oratory and the flowers scattered everywhere? I thought: "How elegantly the words are arranged! How all the little tesserae are set together with art, like a mosaic pavement and an inlaid picture!"

units.la: A sed aliud est Oratorem, aliud Historicum, aliud Theologum agere. Rhetores priscæ elegantiæ oportet esse studiosiores ; Historia res gestas; Theologia demonstrationes ex verbo Dei, & simplicitatem exigunt. Paulus non venit καθ' ὑπεροχὴν λέγω ἢ σοφίας, secundum excellentiam sermonis aut sapientiæ, 1 Cor. 2: 1. non usus est πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις, doctis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως, demonstratione Spiritus & potentiæ. Talem se hoc in tractatu minimè præstat Spanhemius, cujus omnia comicam potius spirant venam, soccos atque cothurnos redolent, quam Euangelicam simplicitatem, Theologo nihilominus ut opinor decorám. Verbis aculeatis, dicteriis, scommatibusque quæ ipsi atra bilis suggessit referta est omnis ipsius pagina, illisque instructa spiculis, quæ iisdem verbis, facili opera, & summo quidem jure in ipsum retorquebunt illi, quos odiosè ubique perstringit, & contra quos Classicum canit. Quæ autem talia sunt, ut eadem opera, qua dicuntur, retorqueri
units.tr: But it is one thing to play the orator, another to play the historian, and another to play the theologian. Rhetoricians must be more devoted to ancient elegance; history demands an account of events; theology demands demonstrations from the Word of God and simplicity. Paul did not come "καθ' ὑπεροχὴν λέγω ἢ σοφίας" [in excellence of speech or of wisdom], "secundum excellentiam sermonis aut sapientiae," 1 Cor. 2:1. He did not use "πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις" [persuasive words of human wisdom], "doctis humanae sapientiae verbis" [with learned words of human wisdom], but "ἀποδείξει πνεύματος καὶ δυνάμεως" [a demonstration of the Spirit and of power], "demonstratione Spiritus et potentiae." Spanheim does not show himself such a man in this treatise. Everything he writes breathes a comic vein, smells of the sock and buskin rather than of evangelical simplicity, though in my opinion simplicity would still become a theologian. His whole page is crammed with biting words, taunts and jibes, drawn from his own spleen, and armed with barbs which, with the same words and with little effort, and indeed with full right, will be turned back upon him by those whom he everywhere assails with malice and against whom he sounds the trumpet call.

units.la: queant in auctores, nihil solidi continere indubium est, atque eo loco suo merito haberi quo anserum strepitus solent, evidens omnium suffragiis judicabitur.
units.tr: There is no doubt that whatever is of such a kind that it can be turned back on its authors, with the same effort by which it is said, contains nothing solid. Its proper place, deservedly, is where the cackling of geese usually is; this will be judged plainly by the votes of all.

units.la: Vult videri dissidiorum sofor, eorumque tranquillus spectator D.Spanhemius, extra partes constitutus, procul omni affectu, amantissimus pacis, qui sine ulla sua culpa ab una diffidentium parte sit passus martyria, quem nemo accusaverit merito suo, cui indies quasi cum belluis sit luctandum. Mirantur certe & stupent docti Novatores, seque in alium propemodum orbem delatos putant. Tam diu nobiscum fuerit Spanhemius, tot ipsis fuerint exedendae contumeliae & injuriae, quas intriverat ille, tot pressi persecutionibus ignorare necesse habeant quo in ipsos sit affectu Dictator iile! rem miram certe & incredibilem. Sed rem ipsam putemus.
units.tr: Spanheim wishes to appear as the peacemaker of the quarrels and their calm spectator, standing apart from the parties, free of all partisanship, a great lover of peace, who through no fault of his own has suffered martyrdom at the hands of one party of the disputants, and whom no one could rightly accuse, while he must wrestle daily as if with wild beasts. Certainly the learned Innovators marvel and are astonished, and think themselves transported into an almost different world. Spanheim has been with us so long, and has had to endure so many insults and injuries, which he himself had brought on; those pressed by his persecutions must needs be ignorant of the feeling with which that Dictator regards them! A strange and incredible thing indeed. But let us take the matter itself as it stands.

units.la: In ipso limine se cum quibusdam consociat quos Fratrum nomine dignatur, & in omni scripto ad eorum causam se adjungit. Hos ab aliis distinguit, contra quos ingemiscit & quiritatur, quibus novaturiendi studium passim tribuit. Ast, an hoc est partes nec facere nec sequi ? an non ita in os contradicit Australis Hollandiæ Synodis Leerdamenfi & Dordracenæ, Annis post natum Salvatorem cıo ıo clxxv. & cıo ıo clxxvi. habitis ? Enimverò in nupera Dordracena Synodo cautum est, ne cuiquam liceat Symmyftas, formulis consensus adhærentes, traducere tamquam Novatores, idque ne fieret publice aut privatim, nec in concionibus nec in Scriptis, nec in Catechisationibus, nec in precibus vel gratiarum actionibus, nec directe vel indirecte, speciali articulo vetitum est. Poftulabant Fratrum quidam in Actis huic articulo adderetut vocula ᴡeᴅᴇr-ȝɧᴅᴡ / ab utraque parte. Morem ipsis gerebant, qui tamen hanc vocem omissam maluissent.
units.tr: At the very threshold he associates himself with certain people whom he deigns to call "Brethren," and in every writing he joins himself to their cause. He distinguishes them from others, against whom he groans and complains, and to whom he everywhere ascribes a zeal for innovation. But is this "neither to make parties nor to follow them"? Does he not contradict to his face the Synods of South Holland, at Leerdam and at Dordrecht, held in the years 1675 and 1676 after the birth of the Saviour? Indeed, at the recent Synod of Dordrecht it was provided, by a special article, that no one might be allowed to slander the Subscribers, who adhere to the formulas of consent, as "Innovators," and that this must not happen "publicly or privately, neither in sermons nor in writings, neither in catechising, nor in prayers or thanksgivings, neither directly nor indirectly." Some of the Brethren asked that the little word wederzijds (on both sides) be added to this article in the Acts. They complied with them, although they would have preferred that this word be left out.

units.la: Sequenti mane Illuftr. Ordinum Deputatus ad Synodum, D. Hudde Synodum monebat, voculam hanc partes hinc inde ponere, proindeque expungendam esse omninò ab iis, qui non tantum (ut ex prælectis Classium votis liquebat) à Schismate, sed ab omni ejus specie erant alieniffi-mi. mi. In hanc Nob D. Deputati sententiam ad unum omnes, & Correspondentes, & Synodi Deputati, & Fratres Synodici, illique ipsi qui additam hanc vocem antea voluerant, unanimi consensu, iverunt, atque etiam pro hac concordia grates Deo folennes à Præside Synodi sunt actæ. Historiam scilicet rerum gestarum procul omni affectu, qua par est fide se Scripturum pollicetur Amico suo Cl. D. Spanhemius. Ast, quare hujus ut & Leerdamensis Synodi acta intacta reliquit dissimulavitque noster Historicus? quare Fratres à Fratribus contra manifestum Synodi decretum distinguit? nisi forte putaverit sic schismatis extruendum sibi esse fundamentum, ad quod procurandum totam hanc comparatam esse epistolam facile qui non admodum obesæ sunt naris, videant & animadvertant. Et tamen inter istos fratres nemo referri queat eorum, qui Synodis Hollandiæ Australis Leerdamensi & Dordracenæ nuperrime interfuere, quorum omnium pacifica fuerunt vota, tolerantiam commendantes sententiæ, & pro tranquillitate Ecclesiastica consilia. Ne inter hos recensere liceat plurimos infinitosque alios pacem cum aliis in quæstioni bus non fundamentalibus amantes memores veteris illius ac tralatitiæ sententiæ,
units.tr: On the following morning the Illustrious Deputy of the Orders to the Synod, Mr. Hudde, advised the Synod that this little word "parties" applies on both sides, and therefore that it must be struck out entirely by those who, as was clear from the declared wishes of the Classes, were not only most remote from schism but from every kind of it. All, with one voice, both the Correspondents and the Deputies of the Synod, and the synodical Brethren, and even those very men who had earlier wished this word to be added, agreed with the opinion of the Deputy; and solemn thanks were rendered to God for this harmony by the President of the Synod. Mr. Spanheim promises, in his letter to his friend, to write a history of these events free of all passion and with the good faith that is proper. But why did our historian leave untouched and pass over in silence the acts of this Synod and of the Synod of Leerdam? Why does he distinguish Brethren from Brethren, against the manifest decree of the Synod? Unless perhaps he thought that a foundation for schism was to be built for himself by this, for the sake of which this whole letter was composed; those whose noses are not too blunt may easily see and notice this. And yet among these brethren no one can be counted who attended the recent Synods of South Holland, at Leerdam and at Dordrecht, all of whose votes were peaceable, commending tolerance of opinion and counsels for ecclesiastical tranquillity. Not to mention the very many and countless others who, in questions that are not fundamental, love peace with others, mindful of that old and common saying,

units.la: Dissentire duos etiam de rebus iisdem Incolumi licuit semper amicitia.
units.tr: "Two men may even disagree about the same things, and friendship remain unharmed."

units.la: Solummodo ergo pro Fratribus hisce Spanhemio dilectis reputandi veniunt illi qui Hagarem expulsam volunt, qui con filiorum de Fratribus exturbandis & deponendis sunt participes. Egregium verò tantis malis Medicum, certè si vulner oleum applicare neglexerit, minimum ic affundet camino. Ita iste verbis nihil quam pacem crepat, quum re ipsa & factis pronus ad pugnas tempestates cieat, bella alat atque adornet, & ad arma viros vocet. Sed de his latius in sequentibus.
units.tr: Only those, therefore, come into account as the Brethren beloved by Spanheim, who want Hagar cast out, who are parties to the plan to drive out and depose the Brethren. Certainly a remarkable physician for such great evils! If he neglects to apply oil to the wound, he will only pour oil on the fire. Thus he chatters of nothing but peace in words, while in deeds and actions he is prone to battles, stirs up storms, feeds and arms wars, and calls men to arms. But more of this at greater length in what follows.

units.la: Atque ea quidem omnia quæ de ipsc verè dici poterant, de iis quos Adversarios elegerat pronuntiavit pro ipsius sc eruditione & modestia. Illos itaque Theologos, à quibus suos Fratres distinguit passim tamquam αὐθάδεις, α᾽πˊπʀs ᾽ς πονηρὸς αὐθρῳ ἀνθρώπους, contentiosos, morosos, implacabiles, indoctos, ὑπερηφάνως, conjurationis reos, Auctoritatis publicæ contemptores, Doctorum virorum æquè ac piorum Osores traducit, atque in eo totus est ut hæc de ipsis Lectori persuadeat. At quo jure? quibus argumentis? lege, perpende totam epistolam, nullam reperies probationem, quam quæ resolvitur in Auctoritatem narrantis, ac si credenda illa forent omnia quia αὐτὸς ἔφα, ipse dixit Dictator Academiarum & Ecclesiarum totius Belgii, alter Papa ex cathedra pronuntians & docens infallibiliter.
units.tr: And all the things that could truly be said about himself, he has pronounced about those whom he had chosen as his opponents, to suit his own learning and modesty. So he brands those theologians, from whom his own brethren are set apart throughout as headstrong, harsh, and wicked men [αὐθάδεις, ἀπηνεῖς, πονηρὸς ἄνθρωπους], as contentious, peevish, implacable, unlearned, proud [ὑπερηφάνως], as guilty of conspiracy, as despisers of public authority, and as haters of learned men no less than of godly ones. He is wholly intent on persuading his reader of these charges. But on what right, and on what arguments? Read the whole letter and weigh it: you will find no proof except what reduces to the authority of the speaker, as if all these things were to be believed because he himself said it [αὐτὸς ἔφα], he himself said it: the Dictator of the Academies and Churches of the whole of Belgium, another Pope, pronouncing and teaching infallibly from the chair.

units.la: Verùm fallor, argumentatur & alicubi, quando scilicet Clarissimi Wittichii Collegæ in speciem honorandi sententiam refert p. 99. &c. & 166. concludituque ipsius dicta occasionem suppeditasse decreto AA. DD. Curatorum, xvi. Januarii. Sed potuisset & hoc labore supersedere, quum jam dudum à plurimis maximèque à Magno D. Heydano demonstratum fuerit in alia omnia torqueri Reverendi Wittichii voces, quam debuerant, neque enim hanc esse vel unquam fuisse Celeberrimi viri sententiam, humanam mentem ad calculos claræ & distinctæ perceptionis revocare aptam natam esse divinitus revelata mysteria, atque adeo res revelatas clare & distincte posse cognoscere, sed hoc velle Theologum vere pacificum, revelationem nos posse clare & distincte percipere, adeoque omni errandi periculo liberari quando fide apprehendimus illa quæ clare & distincte, collatis ponderatisque undique petitis argumentis, percipimus a Deo nobis revelata esse. Quum autem ad istius generis minutias respondsum fit sæpius, neque enim quicquam in integro hoc scripto, in quo tantam pompam adhibuit, reperias quod majoris sit ponderis, prout demonstrare facile erit illis quos istam camarinam movere penitius non pigebit, satius fratrum famæ perciffet Spanhemius, neque bis imo sæpius coctam recoctamque hanc crambem novis verborum phaleris donatam amictamque fastidienti literato orbi denuo propinasset.
units.tr: But I am mistaken: he does argue somewhere, namely when he cites the opinion of the most distinguished Wittichius, his colleague, as if in honour, at pages 99 and following and 166, and concludes that Wittichius's words gave occasion to the decree of the most worthy Curators of 16 January. He might have spared himself this labour, since it has long since been shown by many, and especially by the great Heidanus, that the words of the Reverend Wittichius have been twisted into something other than what they meant. For this was never, nor ever could have been, the opinion of that most celebrated man: that the human mind is by nature fit, by divine gift, to bring revealed mysteries under the scales of clear and distinct perception, and so to know revealed things clearly and distinctly. What a truly peaceable theologian wants to say is this: we can perceive a revelation clearly and distinctly, and so be freed from all danger of error, when by faith we apprehend those things which, after comparing and weighing arguments drawn from every side, we clearly and distinctly perceive to have been revealed to us by God. But since answers to quibbles of this kind have been given many times, and since you will find nothing of weight in this whole writing, in which he has displayed such pomp, as will be easy to show to those who do not shrink from stirring this pot more deeply, Spanheim would have done better to spare his brethren's reputation, and not to have served up to the weary literary world again this cabbage, reheated twice or rather many times, now dressed and draped in new verbal finery.

units.la: At quos viros ab hisce suis Fratribus disjungit ? totos certè paci deditos addictosque , nulli graves , ita à Fratribus quantum ad ea quæ fundamentum non tangunt quandoque dissentientes, ut in disjunctione sententiæ conjuncti tamen amicitia manere studeant optentque, qui cum fe extorta responsione atque inevitabili apologiâ contra inimicorum morsus salsafque delationes & calumnias munire coguntur , lento pede properarunt semper, atque inviti, ut famæ suæ alioquin periclitanti consulerent, adacti sunt ; neque in arenam pertrahi se passi fuissent , nisi minimè fraternos impetus , nemini negato hoc præsidio, propulsare necessarium omninò duxissent. qui certè si per aliquos ipsis non liceat ita gloriari , sedolorem , atque inimicitias suas Ecclesiæ & Reipub. literariæ concessisse , quod magnorum virorum & persapientum esse videtur , hoc tamen jure meritoque possunt uti, quod non tam ad laudem adipiscendam , quam ad vitandam vituperationem valet , nunquam se ullo scripto conten-tio-
units.tr: But from which men does he separate these brethren of his? Surely from men wholly devoted and given to peace, men of no severity, who, though at times differing from their brethren in matters that do not touch the foundation, nevertheless strive and wish to remain friends even while disagreeing in opinion. These men, when forced by an extorted reply and an unavoidable defence against the bites and salty accusations and calumnies of their enemies to protect themselves, have always moved slowly and unwillingly, and have been driven to it only so as to look after their reputation, which was otherwise in danger. Nor would they have allowed themselves to be dragged into the arena, had they not thought it altogether necessary to repel fraternal attacks, a defence that is denied to no one. If they are not permitted, by some men, to boast of this, but are to concede to the Church and the literary commonwealth that they have grief and enmities, which seems to be the mark of great and very wise men, they may nevertheless use this right, justly and deservedly, a right that serves less to win praise than to avoid blame: that they never, in any writing, were contentious, except in so far as certain ambitious brethren, plotting against their reputation and standing even against their will, forced them to it.

units.la: tiosos fuiffe quod non extorferint ipfi etiam nolentibus famæ & exiftimationi ipforum infidiantes papaturientefque quidam Fratres. Ad vos provoco, quibus Ore fcriptifve DD. Heydanus, Coccejus Wittichius, Burmannus, Cartefius, Allinga, cæterique Profeffores Paftorefve quos procul omni ipforum culpâ in hac Epiftola atro carbone notat, innotuerunt, qualefcunque eftis, Tros Rutulufve, Batavi vel Exteri, provoco ad vos, an unquam viros iftos eximios experti fitis tales, quales hic partim aperte partim tecte traducuntur? Teftabitur Belgium, teftabitur omnis Literatus Orbis non minus pacificam Theologiam, folidam Philofophiam, egregiam Literaturam, modeftiam, affabilitatem, comitatem, facilitatem, beneficentiam virorum eruditiffimorum, quam calumnias & machinationes quibus petuntur premunturque à Magiftris quibufdam magis rhetoricantibus quam Prophetantibus aut Philofophantibus. Quorfum autem iftiusmodi ad invidiam compofitis logis & fesquipedalibus verbis ipsorum acta in hunc modum depinguntur? nisi ut inter turbones habeantur, indignationem Magistratuum promeruisse & promereri censeantur, odium plebis ipsis concilietur, & animi Theologorum exterorum contra Innocuos irritentur? quae omnia Deus Opt. Max. benigne avertit hactenus, avertat porro?
units.tr: Contentious they were not, except that certain ambitious brethren, scheming against their reputation and standing, forced them to it even against their will. I call upon you, whoever you are, Trojan or Rutulian, Dutch or foreign, to whom the Reverend Doctors Heidanus, Cocceius, Wittichius, Burmannus, Descartes, Allinga, and the other professors and ministers whom in this letter he brands with black charcoal, far from any fault of theirs, have become known by word or writing: I call upon you to say whether you have ever experienced these outstanding men as they are here openly or covertly depicted. Belgium will testify, and every literate world will testify, to the peaceable theology, the solid philosophy, the excellent learning, and the modesty, affability, courtesy, easiness and beneficence of these most learned men, no less than to the calumnies and machinations by which they are attacked and oppressed by certain teachers who are more rhetorical than prophetic or philosophical. But to what end are their deeds painted in this manner, in sentences composed for odium and in long, high-sounding words? Only so that they may be regarded as troublemakers, that they may be thought to have earned and to deserve the indignation of the magistrates, that hatred of the common people may be stirred against them, and that the minds of foreign theologians may be roused against the innocent? God, the Best and Greatest, has graciously turned all this aside hitherto. May He turn it aside henceforth also!

units.la: Prudentis silentii non pœnitet Spanhomium, siluit ergo usque in hunc diem. Egregium vero silentium, festivam taciturnitatem! quid autem ipsi est siluisse? forte, quod Hulsii multum dilecti fraterculi instar materias controversas non tractaverit. hoc si dicere voluerit, verum quodammodo dixisse eum fatebor, neque id unquam Spanhemium facturum, quae ejus est prudentia, omninò confido. Ast, si per ipsius ad ostentationem jactatum silentium, innuere ipsi animus fit, nunquam se Spanhemium hisce jurgiis atque controversiis immiscuisse, fallit utique Amicum, neque quod res est dicit. Hæc quippe extant internecini odii Spanhemiani specimina & crudelissimæ persecutionis argumenta,
units.tr: Spanheim does not regret a prudent silence: so he has kept silent up to this day. A splendid silence, a festive taciturnity! But what has his silence amounted to? Perhaps that, like his very dear little brother Hulsius, he has not handled the controverted matters. If he means this, I shall admit that he has said something true in a way, and I am wholly confident that Spanheim, with his prudence, would never do otherwise. But if by the silence he boasts of for display he intends to suggest that he has never mixed himself up in these quarrels and controversies, he certainly deceives his friend, and does not say what is the case. For these are plain evidences of Spanheim's implacable hatred and of his most cruel persecution,

units.la: ut frustra quisquam dubitaverit an Spanhemius turbarum rixarumve in Lugdunensi Batava Academia quatuor abhinc annis excitatarum fit primus auctor & per clandestinas artes perpetuus perniciosi illius ignis fotor. Quem enim ipsus sopitum suscitaverat, per alios nutrire maluit, ut gloria sc. silentii maneret ipsi integra.
units.tr: so that no one could doubt for long whether Spanheim was the first author of the disturbances and quarrels stirred up four years ago in the Academy of Leiden, and the constant fomenter of that pernicious fire by secret arts. For the fire he had kindled when it was sleeping he preferred to keep fed through others, so that the glory of silence might remain intact for himself.

units.la: Quis enim primus Anno post Christum natum cIↄ Iↄ cLxxiii. Corollariis suis involavit in Cartesianos tamquam impios quis in Coccejum, quis in Wittichium tamquam Weigelianos? an non Spanhemius in iis quæ subnexa fuere disputationi duodecimæ ad loca illustriora Nov. Test. cum hodiernis Adversariis controversa. Audiantur ipsius voces, & judicet Lector.
units.tr: For who first, in the year of Christ 1673, fell upon the Cartesians with his corollaries as impious? Who fell upon Cocceius, and who upon Wittichius, as a Weigelian? Was it not Spanheim, in those corollaries appended to his twelfth disputation, on the more illustrious passages of the New Testament controverted with present-day adversaries? Let his own words be heard, and let the reader judge.

units.la: I. Dubitare quocunque modo de Dei existentiâ, nec pium est, nec honestum. neque ivit inficias Spanhemius hic à se notatum Cartesium, omnesque norunt hanc sententiam à Spanhemio ipsiusque Fratribus exprobatam sæpissimè Cartesianis fuisse qui poterat igitur hanc sententiam impietatis accusare, nec censeri mordere fratres? tantine ergò erat contra Cartefium paucula hæc verba, à Magno Philosopho & discipulis explicata millies optimaque interpretatione vindicata, in chartas retulisse, ut pacis nulla fuerit habenda ratio, minimèque cavendum ne Fratribus Cartesianis offendiculum præposterâ, detorta atque injuriosâ scriptione poneretur? potuisset utique D. Spanhemius id non agendo omnem offensionem vitasse. Nisi forte Fratrum quorundam, quos honoris pacisque causa hac vice indictos præteribo, instigationibus excitatus, illustri documento probare voluerit, quid pro communi ipsorum causa auderet. Acta refero, nec fabulas scribo, sed talia quæ nobis per ipsius propinquos innotuêre.
units.tr: I. To doubt in any way of God's existence is neither pious nor honourable. Spanheim did not deny that he had marked Descartes with this, and everyone knows that this opinion was very often thrown in the faces of the Cartesians by Spanheim and his brethren. Who, then, could accuse this opinion of impiety without being thought to bite the brethren? Was there so much against Descartes in these few words, explained a thousand times by that great philosopher and his disciples and defended with the best interpretation, that Spanheim had to set them down in writing with no regard for peace, and with no care to avoid putting a stumbling block before his Cartesian brethren by a perverse, twisted and injurious writing? Surely Dr. Spanheim could have avoided all offence by not acting so. Unless, perhaps, spurred on by the instigations of certain brethren, whom I shall pass over for this occasion out of respect and for the sake of peace, he wished to give a striking proof of what he would dare for their common cause. I report facts and do not write fables; these are things that have come to our knowledge through his own relatives.

units.la: Pergit infelix Disputator. II. Angelos non indigere aliquo Ubi in quo existant, & neque hic esse neque illic, male statuit pridem Weigelius. quibus certè verbis Cl. Wittichium notatum atque Weigelianis adscriptum, non dubitabit, qui apprimè edoctus novit illam à Fratribus Spanhemii D. Wittichio sententiam imputatam.
units.tr: The unhappy disputant goes on. II. That angels do not need any place in which they exist, and are neither here nor there: Weigelius long ago stated this wrongly. By these words, surely, Wittichius is marked and assigned to the Weigelians. No one who is well instructed will doubt it, who knows that this opinion was imputed by Spanheim's brethren to Dr. Wittichius.

units.la: Ast, cave credas Lector, sequentibus Corollariis stigma inuri Coccejo, atque etiam hunc minimè contemnendum Theologum à Magno hoc Censore in grege Weigelianorum annumerari. judicat enim fortè honorifice de Celeberrimo Coccejo his verbis, nostra verò hæc est stupiditas ut id non capiamus. III. Male, inquit, cùm idem Weigelius, tum alii, negarunt Patribus Veteris Testamenti Spiritum Adoptionis, & Servitutis tantummodò illum adscripserunt. Neque enim quicquam horum Coccejo fuit imputatum unquam scilicet. Hæc certè fi inspiciantur penitius, & consideretur attentius quid mentita illa belgica (de nodige aentwijfinge &c.) quid in suâ Mantiffa argumentatione vah quàm futili à Coccejo doctum scriptumve frustrà adstruere conatus fuerit Hulfius, Spanhemio profecto Frater tantùm non gemellus, nullo fermè labore & procul omni errandi periculo judicabit omnis, quo jure quâve injuria Spanhemius fe jactet nulli Collegarum injurium, scriptis nullis contentiosum, nullo judicio exactorem rigidum, nulla Hæ-
units.tr: But beware, reader, of believing that by the following corollaries a brand is burned upon Cocceius, or that this theologian, by no means to be despised, is counted by this great censor among the flock of Weigelians. For he judges, perhaps, honourably of the most celebrated Cocceius in these words; but it is our stupidity not to grasp this. III. Wrongly, he says, since the same Weigelius, and others too, denied that the Fathers of the Old Testament had the Spirit of adoption, and ascribed to them only the spirit of bondage. For none of these things was ever imputed to Cocceius, surely. If these matters are examined more closely, and if one considers attentively what that lying Belgic pamphlet (de nodige aentwijfinge, etc.) says, and how vain the argument in his Mantissa is, by which Hulsius tried in vain to establish what Cocceius had taught or written, then anyone, Hulsius being almost a twin brother of Spanheim, will judge with almost no labour and free from all danger of error, by what right, or by what injustice, Spanheim boasts that he is injurious to none of his colleagues, contentious in no writings, a rigid exactor in no judgement, and burdened with no charge of heresy brought by his brethren, and that he has never allowed himself to be dragged into that litigious theatre.

units.la: Hulfius ... (transcribed as printed in the body; the Greek word in the text is rendered as printed: Ἀπόδειξις). Hæreseos accusatione Fratrum gravem, nec in theatrum illud litigiosum pertrahi se unquam passum. Nisi forte hoc profiteri velit, se bello quam paci proniorem, suâ sponte nulla adhibita aliorum vi, nimio revera fervore in pugnam ruisse & in alios cæco impetu incurrisse, & quum adversarium, saltem ex Theologis inveniret nullum, alios in arenam pertraxisse, qui exosos Fratres, ore, scriptis, clamoribus, jurgiis omnique injuriarum genere lacesserent donec ad manus ventum esset. Ita huic & Fratribus ipsius
units.tr: Hulfius ... Apodeixis [Ἀπόδειξις]. Burdened with the accusation of heresy brought by his brethren, and never allowing himself to be dragged into that litigious arena. Unless perhaps he wishes to profess this: that he was more inclined to war than to peace, and rushed into battle of his own accord, with no pressure from others, in a fervour that was truly excessive, and attacked others with blind force; and that, finding no opponent among the theologians, he dragged others into the arena, who assailed his hated brethren with mouth, pen, shouting and quarrels, and with every kind of insult, until it came to blows. So it was for him and his brethren.

units.la: Bella geri placuit, nullos habitura triumphos, & in propria viscera sævire religio non fuit.
units.tr: It was decided to wage war, though it would bring no triumphs, and it was no scruple to rage against one's own vitals.

units.la: Inspiciantur & quæ corollaria illa quæ supra citavi sequuntur, & palam fiet, illa omnia opposita fuisse sententiæ quæ affingitur illis, quos à Fratribus suis disjunctos vult.
units.tr: Let the corollaries I cited above, and what follows them, be examined, and it will be plain that they all stand opposed to the opinion that is attributed to those whom he wishes to be separated from their brethren.

units.la: Hæc sunt verba. IV. Christus fuit plenarius Expromissor, seu Interventor, adeoque Redemptor sub V. T. à Deo creditore nostro tum datus tum acceptatus. V. Expromissionis ejus is fuit effectus, etiam ante actualem solutionem, sed tamen certam & necessariam, ut liberati fuerint peccatores credentes sub V. Test.
units.tr: These are his words. IV. Christ was the full Surety, or Intercessor, and so the Redeemer under the Old Testament, given and accepted by God as our creditor. V. The effect of this suretyship was also present before the actual payment, but still certain and necessary, so that believing sinners were set free under the Old Testament.

units.la: VI. Hæc liberatio dici potest tum παρεσις, seu prætermissio, vel dimissio primi debitoris; tum ἀφεσις, seu remissio debiti, ob translationem ejus in alium; tum ἀνεσις seu relaxatio; tum ἀθωωσις seu liberatio, absolutio; tum acceptilatio, non imputatio, non punitio &c. promiscuo usu vocum in & extra Scripturam sacram.
units.tr: VI. This liberation may be called παρεσις [paresis], that is, passing over or dismissal of the first debtor; also ἀφεσις [aphesis], that is, remission of the debt, on account of its transfer to another; also ἀνεσις [anesis], that is, relaxation; also ἀθωωσις [athoōsis], that is, deliverance, absolution; also acceptilatio, non-imputation, non-punishment, etc., these words being used interchangeably within and outside holy Scripture.

units.la: VII. Non intercedit illi liberationi vel remissioni, conscientia peccatorum, de qua Paulus ad Hebr. 10: 2. nec commemoratio eorundem ad Hebr. 10: 3. nec chirographum nondum abolitum, ὃ καθ' ἡμῶν, ad Coloss. 11: 14. quibus sane respexit Paulus ad ipsam solutionem, seu expiationem adhuc actu præstandam ab Expromissore, & quoque ad usum oblationum sub V. T. earumque ἀσθενειαν και ἀδυναμίαν.
units.tr: VII. There did not stand in the way of that liberation or remission the consciousness of sins, of which Paul speaks in Hebrews 10:2, nor the remembrance of them in Hebrews 10:3, nor the handwriting not yet abolished, which was against us, in Colossians 2:14. By these Paul surely had regard to the payment itself, or the expiation still to be actually made by the Surety, and also to the use of the sacrifices under the Old Testament and their weakness and powerlessness [ἀσθένειαν καὶ ἀδυναμίαν].

units.la: VIII. Indubium tamen est majorem jam esse sub N. T. (post præstitam solutionem, abolitum chirographum, adeoque post peremptam substantiam debiti & post discussas umbras) παῤῥησίαν, χαρὰν, καύχησιν.
units.tr: VIII. Yet it is beyond doubt that under the New Testament there is greater confidence, joy and boasting [παρρησίαν, χαρὰν, καύχησιν], now that the payment has been made, the handwriting abolished, and therefore the substance of the debt destroyed and the shadows dispelled.

units.la: Defensa sunt illa Corollaria ad diem 10. Junii. Parvo post tempore primo Corollario de Dubitatione agenti, aliud opposuit Cl. D. Cranen, tunc temporis Philosophiæ Professor atque Illustr. Ord. Hollandiæ Collegii Subregens, quo injuriam à Spanhemio Cartesio ipsiusque Discipulis factam repelleret, aculeatis fateor dictis. Erat tunc Academiæ Rector Spanhemius, propria auctoritate prohibet illam defendi disputationem, & quod omni caret exemplo, factumque contra Leges Academiæ, affixum titulum avelli curat. Hinc contentio inter Ipsum & D. Cranen, qui jussis parere recusat atque Disputationem invito Spanhemio defendit. At quæ non hinc contra D. Cranen querelæ & lamentationes in sinum Ampliss. DD. Curatorum effusæ, quibus non vocibus flebilibus spretam auctoritatem, illatasque ut opinabatur injurias vindicandas petiit, obtinuitque!
units.tr: Those corollaries were defended on 10 June. Shortly afterwards, when the first corollary, on Doubt, was under discussion, the distinguished Mr. Cranen, then Professor of Philosophy and Sub-Regent of the Illustrious College of the Order of Holland, put forward another, by which he repelled the injury done by Spanheim to Descartes and his disciples, with stinging words, I admit. Spanheim was then Rector of the Academy. On his own authority he forbade that disputation to be defended, and, which has no precedent and was contrary to the laws of the Academy, he had the posted title torn down. Hence a quarrel between himself and Mr. Cranen, who refused to obey the order and defended the disputation against Spanheim's wishes. But what complaints and lamentations were then poured into the bosom of the most distinguished Curators against Mr. Cranen! With tearful words he sought, and obtained, that his scorned authority and the injuries he supposed had been done to him should be avenged!

units.la: Rogaverit jam quisquam, qua occasione aliquo post tempore D. Cranen Collegium Ampliff. DD. Ordinum Hollandiæ Professionemque Philosophicam deferere jussus fit, non mediocri cum jactura salarii ad Professionem Medicam vocatus? hoc profecto respondi feret. occasione delationis perpetuæ à Spanhemio ejusque affeclis id factum, nescit nemo.
units.tr: Let anyone now ask on what occasion, some time later, Mr. Cranen was ordered to give up the College of the Most Distinguished Orders of Holland and the chair of Philosophy, and was called to the chair of Medicine with no small loss of salary. Surely the answer will be: no one knows, except that it was done on account of the perpetual delation by Spanheim and his partisans.

units.la: Quis quicquid adversi ipsi contingeret, quis factas sibi injurias, quis illatas sibi contumelias, à Studiosis aliisque quorum irritaverat iras, quorum omnium animos inhumana crudelique austeritate, indigna contemptione ac despicientia, impotentique dominatu quem non tantum in omnis generis studiosos sed & in Collegas exercebat superbissimè, à se alienaverat, imputavit Collegis, atque hoc nomine apud Ampliff. DD. Curatores eos accusavit? an non Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who imputed to his colleagues whatever adversity befell him, whatever injuries were done to him, whatever insults were offered him, by students and others whose anger he had provoked, and whose minds he had alienated from himself by his inhuman and cruel severity, by his undeserved contempt and scorn, and by the domineering power he exercised most arrogantly not only over students of every kind but also over his colleagues; and who on this ground accused them before the Most Distinguished Curators? Was it not Spanheim?

units.la: Quis Epistolam ad Hebræos publicè prælecturus applicatamque daturus, id ferè unicè egit, ut Commentarium Cl. Cocceji refutatum daret, nec sincerâ atque Theologo dignâ fide Cl. Viri fentensiam semper referens? Quis in Collegiis ita Locos communes Theologicos tractavit, ut quæ hodiè finguntur esse controversa, sola fermè attigerit, cæteris tantum non neglectis? Utique Spanhemius, si perplurimorum Auditorum dictis narratisque fidem adhibere liceat.
units.tr: Who, when about to lecture publicly on the Epistle to the Hebrews and to give a dictation, did almost nothing but give a refutation of Cocceius's commentary, and did not always report the opinion of that distinguished man with the sincere and theologically worthy good faith it deserved? Who, in his lectures, treated the common topics of theology in such a way that he touched almost only on those matters which are today fabricated as controversial, while the rest were scarcely neglected? Spanheim, surely, if we may give credence to the words and reports of very many hearers.

units.la: Quis præsentibus Collegis, quum ob excitatos in Disputatione D. de Vries tumultus, ut criminis causæ delati essent, & à DD. Curatoribus vocati ut se defenderent, quasi ipsius causa ageretur, dixit se amplius docere non posse, si illa Philosophia, Cartesianam innuens, traderetur ulterius? Nonne is fuit D. Spanhemius? Quâ fronte igitur querulum hoc caput profiteatur se nulli Collegarum injurium?
units.tr: Who, in the presence of his colleagues, when because of the tumults stirred up in the disputation of Mr. de Vries the men were denounced as guilty and summoned by the Curators to defend themselves, as if the case were about him, said that he could no longer teach if that philosophy, hinting at the Cartesian, were taught any further? Was it not Mr. Spanheim? With what face, then, does he now profess in this querulous chapter that he is injurious to none of his colleagues?

units.la: Sub finem Anni cIↄ Iↄ cLxxiv. D. Spanhemius Disputationi nî fallor nonæ de Statu & Luctâ Hominis Regeniti, hæc corollaria annexa dederat,
units.tr: Near the end of the year 1674, Mr. Spanheim, if I am not mistaken, had attached these corollaries to his ninth disputation, On the State and Struggle of the Regenerate Man:

units.la: I. Differentia inter œconomiam Veteris & illam N. T. consistit potissimum in externa administratione Fœderis gratiæ
units.tr: I. The difference between the economy of the Old and that of the New Testament consists chiefly in the external administration of the covenant of grace.

units.la: quæ administratio illic rigidior, operosior, obscurior, hic suavior, facilior clarior, illic magis restricta & limitata, hic vero amplior magisque extensa.
units.tr: That administration was there more rigid, laborious and obscure; here it is sweeter, easier and clearer; there it was more restricted and limited, here it is broader and more extended.

units.la: II. Neutiquam verò discrepantia illa quærenda in donis salutiferis, justificatione, adoptione, sanctificatione, charitate, inscriptione legis in cordibus, pace cum Deo, tranquillitate conscientiæ, quæ charismata utrobique eadem.
units.tr: II. By no means is that difference to be sought in the saving gifts, justification, adoption, sanctification, love, the writing of the law in the hearts, peace with God, and tranquillity of conscience, which graces are the same in both.

units.la: III. Nec aliter fieri potuit, quia utrobique per fidem conscientiis fuit applicatum unum idemque meritum efficacissimum, pretium sc. sanguinis Filii Dei, sive jam in carne exhibiti sive exhibendi.
units.tr: III. Nor could it have been otherwise, because in both cases one and the same most efficacious merit was applied by faith to consciences, namely the price of the blood of the Son of God, whether already manifested in the flesh or yet to be manifested.

units.la: Ex hisce profesto Corollariis eorumque comparatione cum prioribus videre erat, non constare sibi D. Spanhemium atque in pejus eum proficere; siquidem priori disputatione agnovit sub N. Test. majorem esse παρρησίαν, χαράν, καύχησιν, atque in posteriori asseruit discrepantiam inter Oeconomiam Veteris & illam N. Test. non esse quærendam in donis salutiferis, justificatione, adoptione, sanctificatione, charitate, inscri-ptione ptione legis in cordibus, pace cum Deo, tranquillitate conscientiæ, quæ charismata utrobique eadem. Verùm, hæc transeant cum cæteris erroribus, forte è re sua putavit sententiam mutare, quo liberius posset fratribus contradicere. Nactus illâ horâ erat opponentem D. Cornelium vander Linden, Medicinæ Doctorem & Minifterii Candidatum, imparatum tamen nec quicquam istiusmodi meditatum atque in ipso Auditorio casu in hæc corollaria incidentem. Lis tunc brevis erat, instabat enim hora. Tempore interclusus Opponens, quo minus quæ in promptu ipsi erant argumenta proferret, destitit. Urgebat D. Spanhemius, sibi satisfactum diceret. recusavit alter, nec eo adduci se passus est. Provocavit eum Spanhemius, ut proxima disputatione se sisteret, curaturus eadem reponerentur argumenta. Fidem dedit Opponens. Stetit promissis D. Spanhemius, nec partibus suis defuit D. vander Linden, non parum indignans quod post primam oppositionem in Fabula Acceptilationis nullo suo merito à D. Spanhemio, (qui jam antea Magnificus Rector eum omni injuria, gradum Doctoratus petentem, non fine ignominia atque infamia prohibita disputationis Medicæ, quam conscripserat Candidatus nimis ex fententia Cartefii, quasi plena effet dubitationum, defensione, affecerat,) livido dente fe morsum comperiret. Quid fit? defcendunt in certamen uterque septimo decimo Kal. Febr. Anni cıɔ ıɔ cLxxv. congrediuntur, ad incitas redigitur Cl. Spanhemius non semel, dicta revocat atque indicta asserit, urget Opponens dictaque repetit; Calumniatorem eum dicit Spanhemius, Opponens convitium reddit optimæque fidei quotquot aderant Auditores Spectatoresque testes citat, Spanhemius verborum atque argutiarum fuliginem ob oculos audientium jacit, & tandem audita hora separantur. Quæ certè ita gesta esse omnia, nemo qui à præjudiciis liber disputationi interfuit, negabit. Unde facile est judicare quàm verè D. Spanhemius afferat fe nunquam in istud Theatrum litigiosum pertrahi fe passum; qui provocavit prior virum, à quo quid meritus effet noverat optimè, nec provocavit tantùm, sed & maledictis lacessivit prior, atque irritavit denuò. Quis autem Disputatione finitâ contra D. vander Linden, imploravit atque impetravit Ampliff. D D. Curatorum opem, ac si non argumentis sed injuriis & convitiis ab eo petitus fuisset? nec tantum contra hunc, sed & contra D. Bontekoe Medicinæ itidem Doctorem, quasi hic priorem continuis instigationibus juvisset, quamvis D. vander Linden negaret id ullo modo factum, assereretque non observatum sibi D. Bontekoe initio Disputationis fuisse vicinum, nec ullum ipsius verbum aures suas percussisse jurare paratus esset. Ast, factis jam sæpius probaverat quid posset contra Peripateticos, jamque sentiendum ipsi erat, quantum referret iram Spanhemii subiisse. Verùm, an non hæc omnia ad Ampliff. D D. Curatorum aures retulit querula vox Spanhemii?
units.tr: From these corollaries, and from their comparison with the earlier ones, it was plain indeed that Mr. Spanheim was not consistent with himself and was progressing for the worse. For in the earlier disputation he acknowledged that under the New Testament there is greater confidence [παρρησίαν], joy [χαρὰν], and boasting [καύχησιν], while in the later one he asserted that the difference between the economy of the Old Testament and that of the New is not to be sought in the saving gifts, justification, adoption, sanctification, love, the writing of the law in the hearts, peace with God, and tranquillity of conscience, which graces are the same in both. But let these things pass along with his other errors. Perhaps he thought it was to his advantage to change his opinion, so that he might contradict his brethren more freely. At that hour he found as opponent Mr. Cornelius van der Linden, Doctor of Medicine and candidate for the ministry, who was unprepared and had considered nothing of the kind, and who had by chance fallen upon these corollaries in the lecture hall itself. The dispute was then brief, for the hour was pressing. The opponent, cut short by the time, stopped short of producing the arguments he had ready. Spanheim pressed him to say that he was satisfied; the other refused and would not allow himself to be brought to it. Spanheim challenged him to appear at the next disputation, promising that the same arguments would be taken up again. The opponent gave his word. Mr. Spanheim kept his promise, and Mr. van der Linden did not fail in his part, being not a little indignant that after the first opposition, in the Fable of Acceptilation, he found himself bitten with a spiteful tooth by Mr. Spanheim, without any merit of his own. (Spanheim, who as Magnificent Rector had earlier treated him with every injury, when he sought the degree of Doctor, forbidding him, not without disgrace and infamy, to defend the medical disputation he had written as a candidate, on the ground that it was too much in accord with Descartes and full of doubts.) What happened? Both descended into the contest on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February in the year 1675. They met; Mr. Spanheim was driven to fury more than once, retracting what he had said and asserting what he had not said; the opponent pressed on and repeated his words; Spanheim called him a slanderer; the opponent returned the insult and called on all the hearers and spectators present, men of the best faith, as witnesses; Spanheim threw the smoke of words and quibbles before the eyes of the audience; and at last, when the hour was up, they parted. No one who attended the disputation free from prejudice will deny that all this was indeed so. From this it is easy to judge how truly Mr. Spanheim asserts that he has never allowed himself to be dragged into that litigious theatre; for he was the first to challenge the man, whom he knew very well how he had treated, and he not only challenged him but was the first to assail him with abuse, and again provoked him. Who, after the disputation was over, sought and obtained the help of the Most Distinguished Curators against Mr. van der Linden, as if he had been attacked not with arguments but with injuries and insults? And not only against him, but also against Mr. Bontekoe, likewise Doctor of Medicine, as if the latter had aided the first by continual instigations, although Mr. van der Linden denied that this had been done in any way, and declared that Bontekoe had not been near him at the beginning of the disputation, and was ready to swear that no word of his had struck his ears. But he had already often proved by deeds what he could do against the Peripatetics, and now it was for him to feel how much it mattered to have incurred Spanheim's anger. Yet did not that querulous voice of Spanheim carry all these things to the ears of the Most Distinguished Curators?

units.la: Quis Concionatores, viam pacis explicantes, ægerrimè atque <bl>ἀταξία</bl> ad scandalum usque, audivit, & postea tanquam Turbones passim denigrare atque infamare non est veritus? an non Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who has heard the preachers, who were explaining the way of peace, attacked most bitterly and to the point of scandal and disorder [ἀταξία], and then did not hesitate to denigrate and defame them everywhere as troublemakers? Did Spanhemius not?

units.la: Quis publicè in Academia Venerando D. Heydano præsenti in Disputatione Medica Inaugurali D. Hermanni Bruynfteen, & amicè atque familiariter cum ipso de objectione quadam Opponentis secundum hypotheses Cartefii loquenti, iracundâ atque altâ satis voce, lites movit de Philosophia Cartesiana à cancellis Theologicis ablegSanda, & quum indomita ipsius verba vir magnus frangere conaretur, mendacium quod res erat dicenti Seni, rusticâ voce exprobravit? an non pro suâ modestiâ Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who, at a public disputation in the Academy, in the presence of the venerable Dr. Heydanus, during the inaugural medical disputation of Dr. Hermann Bruynsteen, when a certain objection of the opponent, who was speaking according to the hypotheses of Descartes, was being discussed in a friendly and familiar way with him, raised a quarrel in an angry and rather loud voice, declaring that the Cartesian philosophy must be banished from the theological enclosures; and when that great man tried to break off his unrestrained words, reproached the old man, in a rustic voice, with lying, though what he said was true? Did Spanhemius not, for all his modesty?

units.la: Quis contradictionem ferre nescius apud Curatores & Ampliff. Ordines Frisiæ contra Bekkerum, apud Antistitem Helvetium nuper contra D. Switserum flebiles anilesque questus fudit? an non Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who, unable to bear contradiction, poured out tearful and old-womanish complaints before the curators and the honourable orders of Friesland against Bekker, and recently before the Swiss antistes against Dr. Swyser? Did Spanhemius not?

units.la: Quis in concionibus Gallicis; quæ prosecto non recitantur gratis, tam Leydæ quam Hagæ Comitis contra Auctorem scripti de Lumine, Philosophosque modernos dernos debacchatus est quam maximè impotenter atque contumeliose? An non Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who raged, most violently and insultingly, in the French sermons, which are certainly not given free of charge, at Leiden as well as at The Hague, against the author of the writing on Light and against the modern philosophers? Did Spanhemius not?

units.la: Quis ad interrogata D. Hulfii de sententia magni Spanhemii Patris circa discrimen V. & N. T. fatis acerbè in dictos Novatores invectus respondit per literas, ea procul dubio lege, ut epistola illa Thesibus extraordinariis D. Hulfii inserta profiaret publicè? an non D. Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who, in answer to the questions of Dr. Hulsius about the opinion of the great Spanheim his father on the difference between the Old and New Testaments, inveighed rather bitterly against the said innovators in a letter, undoubtedly on the condition that that letter, inserted in Dr. Hulsius's extraordinary theses, should be published? Did not Dr. Spanheim?

units.la: Quis ex Cocceji scriptis, ex Wittichii Theologia Pacifica aliisque laboribus pessimè detorta verba excerpsit sub finem Anni cIↄ Iↄ cLXXv. interfuitque comitiis eorum, si non præfuit, qui Catalogos hæresefeon contra symmiftas texuere, exhibendos Proceribus iisque qui Reipub. gubernacula tenent, impertiendos Fratribus suis & cum iis communicandos in quorum & hodiè sunt manibus? qui certè si non sola, saltem primaria causa fuerunt Decreti a. d. xvi. Januarii Anni cIↄ Iↄ cLXXvI. promulgati? Utique Spanhemius.
units.tr: Who, from the writings of Coccejus, from Wittichius's Pacific Theology, and from other works, extracted words most wickedly twisted, toward the end of the year 1675, and took part in the assemblies of those who, if they did not preside over them, drew up the catalogues of heretics against the sympathisers, to be presented to the nobles and those who hold the reins of government, and to be handed over to his brothers and shared with those into whose hands they are still passed today? Those who, if not the sole cause, were certainly the primary cause of the decree promulgated on 16 January 1676? Certainly Spanheim.

units.la: Quis Leidâ Hagam profecturus, in itinere pofeffus est, se totum in eo esse, omnemque lapidem movere, ut pellerentur novitates illæ? an non Spanhemius?
units.tr: Who, setting out from Leiden for The Hague, declared on the journey that he was wholly bent on this, and would move every stone so that those novelties might be driven out? Did Spanheim not?

units.la: Hæc Lugduni in Batavis lippis & tonsoribus notissima sunt. Plura Deus novit & ipse conscius sibi est Spanhemius, atque dies forte docebit. Historias edere eorum erit, quos hæc pericopa propius tangit: nunc sufficiat ostendisse, minimè vera esse quæ Spanhemius de suo non pænitendo silentio prædicat.
units.tr: These things are very well known at Leiden among the bleary-eyed Dutch and the barbers. God knows more, and Spanheim is conscious of them himself, and perhaps the day will teach more. It will be the task of those whom this passage concerns more closely to relate the histories; for now it is enough to have shown that what Spanheim proclaims about his unrepentant silence is by no means true.

units.la: Ast, quid jam hisce omnibus reponet Spanhemius? negabit forte quicquam horum esse factum confidens pios illos viros coram quibus omnia hæc acta sunt non facilè passuros se in partes vocari, potiusque publici testimonii invidiam quamdiu id fieri poterit, fugituros; quæ Fratrum persecutorum perpetuæ sunt artes. Verùm sic omnia & cordis penetralia lustrantem Deum non decipiet, si forte hominibus rerum ignaris imponet, & majorem faciet vim conscientiæ.
units.tr: But what will Spanheim now reply to all these things? Perhaps he will deny that any of them happened, confidently asserting that those pious men in whose presence all these things were done would not easily allow themselves to be called upon as witnesses, and would, for as long as it is possible, shun the odium of public testimony; these are the perpetual arts of the persecutors of the brethren. But God, who searches all the secrets of the heart, will not be deceived by this, even if he imposes upon men ignorant of the facts, and he will make the force of conscience greater.

units.la: Porrò parallela simillimaque fingit dicta factaque exosorum Fratrum, Remonstrantiumque olim prætextus. Hoc enim
units.tr: Moreover, he invents parallels, and very similar to these, with the words and deeds of the hated brethren, the Remonstrants of former times, as a pretext. For he does this

units.la: à pag. 21. ad pag. 31. usque agit, vel nihil agit. Idque, ut hanc Lectorum animis tacitam insinuet conclusionem, simili modo cum his agendum, quo actum fuit cum Arminianis Remonstrantibus: removendos à Scholis & Cathedris Academicis, Ecclesiâ pellendam domoque ejiciendam hanc Hagarem, ut solus dominetur inter suos Fratres persecutores Dictator futurus perpetuus. Provocarunt Remonstrantes ad formulas Consensus, conquesti sunt de inquisitione & tyrannide & Magisterio quorundam in Belgio. Commendarunt tolerantiam in quæstionibus de V. articulus, urserunt libertatem prophetandi, profectum & multiplicationem cognitionis commendarunt &c. Idem autem dicunt atque agunt hodierni Theologi cum quibus Spanhemio & Fratribus ipsius res est. Quid inde! Ergo Remonstrantes sunt aut Remonstrantium hypothesi affiniores ? λόγοι, ineptiæ. An quando duo dicunt idem, id semper revera est idem? Hoc utique artificio Unusquisque omnes obtestationes, prote-sta-
units.tr: from page 21 to page 31, or does nothing at all. And he does this so that he may insinuate into the minds of the readers the silent conclusion that they should be dealt with in the same way as the Arminian Remonstrants were: removed from the schools and academic chairs, the Church to be driven out and this Hagar cast out of the house, so that he alone may rule among his brethren, the persecutors, as a perpetual dictator. The Remonstrants appealed to the formulas of consensus; they complained of the inquisition, the tyranny and the magisterium of certain men in Belgium. They commended tolerance in questions about the fifth article; they urged freedom of prophesying; they commended progress and the multiplication of knowledge, and so on. Yet today's theologians, with whom Spanheim and his brethren have their dispute, say and do the same things. What follows from this? Are they therefore Remonstrants, or closer to the Remonstrant position? Empty words, nonsense! Or when two men say the same thing, is it always really the same thing? By this trick anyone at all can make the oaths, protestations

units.la: stationes subscriptionesque Fratrum su\ spectas habere potis est ; nec erit, quo\ vir probus vel honestiorum quisquam si\ dem facere atque impetrare queat.
units.tr: protestations and subscriptions of the brethren suspect; and no upright man, nor any of the more honourable, will be able to give or obtain credit.

units.la: In eundem hunc modum [illegible, ~3 letters] coram componunt comparantque Papistæ aliique Calvinianos ut vocant Reforma\ tos & Turcas , Protestantes & veteri\ Ecclesiæ hæreticos. Remonstrantes po\ tuerunt generalia quædam juris adferre quæ si simpliciter considerentur sunt ve\ rissima, perperam vero applicata veri ni\ hil dicunt. Quid an non datur in cogni\ tione profectus? an scientiæ multiplica\ tio non est promissa? an non est prophe\ tandum ? an Mortalium quisquam Magi\ ster fidei esse queat? an autoritatem hu\ manam in judicio Ecclesiastico prævaler\ æquum est? nonne [illegible, ~4 letters] recteque de\ Deo atque ejus verbo sentiens Theologu\ se iis opponere necesse habet, qui tyran\ nidem & nomen humanum in Ecclesian\ reducere omnibus viribus nituntur? vide\ hic generalia quædam juris, quæ uniuscu\ jusque conscientiæ quam maximè obvi\sunt sunt, quæ licet à Remonstrantibus falso peffimæ causæ fuerint prætenfa, nihilominus ab aliis oportunè admodum summoque cum jure allegari possunt. Tamdiu itaque nihil egerit Spanhemius, instar eorum qui αἱρὰ δἰρεσι, quam diu non probaverit invictis argumentis hæc effata ab exosis Fratribus prætendi magis, quam rectè ipsorum causæ applicari.
units.tr: In this same manner [illegible, ~3 letters] the Papists and others set side by side and compare the so-called Calvinian reformed with the Turks, and the Protestants with the heretics of the ancient Church. The Remonstrants could bring forward certain general principles of law which, if considered in themselves, are most true, but which, wrongly applied, say nothing true. What then? Is there no room for progress in knowledge? Is the multiplication of knowledge not promised? Is it not to be prophesied? Can any mortal be a master of faith? Is it right that human authority should prevail in ecclesiastical judgement? Must not a theologian who thinks rightly of God and of his Word necessarily oppose those who strive with all their might to bring tyranny and human name back into the Church? [illegible, ~4 letters] Here are certain general principles of law, which are most opposed to the conscience of each individual; and although they were falsely pretended by the Remonstrants for a most wretched cause, they can nevertheless be fittingly and with great justice alleged by others. Therefore Spanheim will have accomplished nothing, like those who choose heresies [αἱρέσεις], as long as he has not proved by invincible arguments that these sayings, put forward by the hated brethren, are more a pretence than a correct application to their cause.

units.la: Sed jugulandus venit Spanhemius suo ferro. Strinxit enim in proprium jugulum hunc gladium. Examinare igitur liceat in quibus hujus Fratrumque ejus persecutorum acta cum Remonstrantium gestis conveniant. Arminiani anxiè ambierunt Operam favoremque Magistratus tam summi quam subalterni: idem agunt Spanhemius ejusque Fratres. Arminiani silentium imponi Orthodoxis à Magistratu postulaverunt: idem petunt Spanhemius ejusque Fratres. Arminiani provocarunt ad Antiquitatem & Veterum consensum; idem agunt D. Spanhemius ejusque Fratres, Novitatis accusantes symmystas. Arminiani Orthodoxos tamquam Turbones, indoctos, eruditioni inimicos fugillarunt: idem agit Spanhemius hoc in scripto. Arminiani volebant videri urgere praxin pietatis, vociferatique sunt non laborandum de spinosis controversiis, quas logomachias vocabant, sed de moribus emendandis multa jactabant: idem clamant Spanhemius atque ejus Fratres persecutores. Arminiani pacis gratia scilicet, liberam obtulerunt ministeriorum desertionem: idem si non obtulerit, laudat minimum Spanhemius in hac eadem Epistola. Plura studio omittimus, neque enim necesse est omnia talia corradere: sufficiunt hæc pauca ad monendum Spanhemium, istius generis lenociniis imponi non posse oculatis.
units.tr: But Spanheim comes to be slaughtered with his own sword, for he has drawn this sword against his own throat. Let us therefore examine in what respects the actions of him and of his persecuting brethren agree with the deeds of the Remonstrants. The Arminians eagerly sought the favour and help of the magistrate, both high and low; Spanheim and his brethren do the same. The Arminians demanded that the Orthodox be ordered by the magistrate to keep silence; Spanheim and his brethren ask for the same. The Arminians appealed to antiquity and the consensus of the Fathers; Spanheim and his brethren do the same, accusing their fellow-sympathisers of novelty. The Arminians disparaged the Orthodox as troublemakers, the unlearned, enemies of learning; Spanheim does the same in this writing. The Arminians wished to seem to press the practice of piety, and they cried out that one should not labour over thorny controversies, which they called logomachies, but boasted much about reforming morals; Spanheim and his persecuting brethren shout the same. The Arminians, for the sake of peace, of course offered the free desertion of their ministries; if Spanheim has not offered this, he at least praises it in this same letter. We omit many things deliberately, for it is not necessary to collect all such things; these few are enough to warn Spanheim that men with their eyes open cannot be deceived by blandishments of this kind.

units.la: Fortunas suas deplorat, de injuriis contumeliisque sibi illatis conqueritur, & tantum non vulnera narrat. Ipsius vicem quis non doleat! Gaudet duplici Professoratu, Theologiæ sc. & Sacræ Historiæ: quadruplex accipit stipendium, quorum primum ei confertur pro Theologiæ, secundum pro S. Historiæ Professoratu, tertium pro munere Bibliothecarii, quartum pro concionibus Gallicis singulis mensibus habendis. Gaudet favore Magnatum & Nobiliff. DD. Curatorum: quinimo non ita pridem impetravit ut singulis septimanis, non ut antea sexies, quater Theologiam, diebusque feriatis Ecclesiasticam Historiam, sed quater tantum alternis vicibus Theologiam, alternis vero Historias docendas habeat, diebusque feriatis ferietur. vix igitur credibile eo Spanhemium respexisse, nisi ingratissimum se praedicare voluisset.
units.tr: He laments his fortunes, complains of the injuries and insults inflicted on him, and almost recounts his wounds. Who would not grieve for his plight! He rejoices in a double professorship, of theology and of sacred history; he receives a fourfold stipend, of which the first is paid to him for the professorship of theology, the second for the professorship of sacred history, the third for the office of librarian, and the fourth for holding French sermons each month. He rejoices in the favour of the magnates and the honourable curators. Indeed, not long ago he obtained that, instead of teaching theology six times a week, as before, and church history on holidays, he should teach theology four times, and only on alternate occasions teach theology and on alternate occasions history, and that he should have holidays. It is therefore hardly credible that Spanheim had this in mind, unless he wished to proclaim himself most ungrateful.

units.la: Alio igitur oculos retulisse Spanhemium oportet, innuitque fortasse contumelias injuriasve in famosis libellis ipsi impositas; aut convitia nonnunquam ipsi a male feriatis quibusdam juvenibus dicta: forte & tyrannidem ipsi non frustra in anonymis quibusdam scriptis imputatam. Vah quanta martyria! Spanhemii Fratres si non & ipse fatis functo atque ad meliora evocato Coccejo <bl>ἀλγοῦντες</bl> & haeretici famam inurere conati sunt. Acerbiora certe fata lugent Ven. D. Heydanus, D. Wittichius, D. Burmannus, D. Crannen, Dr. vander Linden, D. Swartenhengst, atque altiores plagas accepere, quibus auctoribus atque proxenetis ipse novit Spanhemius & ex parte supra visum est. Spanhemii vero passiones, si quae sint, verbis terminantur, quae nec crumenae nec corpori nocent; & si quo modo praepostero imperandi studio nimiaque vel inhumana austeritate propriam famam laeserit, poterit ingenuo nec fucato amore, comitate atque humanitate omnia emendare atque e comtemptibus exire.
units.tr: Spanheim must therefore have turned his eyes elsewhere, and perhaps he hints at insults or injuries imposed on him in libellous pamphlets, or at abuse sometimes hurled at him by certain badly brought up young men; perhaps also at tyranny imputed to him, not without reason, in certain anonymous writings. Alas, what great martyrdoms! Spanheim's brethren, if not Spanheim himself, have tried to brand Coccejus, now dead and called to better things, as a heretic and a man grieving [ἀλγοῦντες]. Certainly the venerable Dr. Heydanus, Dr. Wittichius, Dr. Burmann, Dr. Crannen, Dr. van der Linden, Dr. Swartenhengst mourn harsher fates, and have received deeper wounds, by whose authors and go-betweens Spanheim himself knows, and this has been partly shown above. But Spanheim's sufferings, if there are any, end in words, which harm neither purse nor body; and if he has in any way damaged his own reputation through a perverse zeal for command and excessive or even inhuman severity, he can, with a sincere and unfeigned love, kindness and courtesy, correct everything and emerge from contempt.

units.la: Libellos famosos tumultusque Academicos exosi Fratres ex animo detestantur, magisque a talibus abhorrent quam forte ipse D. Spanhemius, quem jam didicisse istius generis chartas contemnere, sperant. Atque eo magis vellent a talibus abstineri, quod alienandis ab invicem Fratrum voluntatibus atque animis, non sic ut par erat conjunctis, apta nata sint atque unice inserviant. Verum est, male audit Cl. D. Spanhemius a plerisque studiosorum. rogaverit vero quisquam quæ tantarum irarum fit causa; regerunt illico, tristi severitate in vultu, torvo lumine, ingenio sævo, inhumano atque inquieto, iracundia, avaritia, superbia, ambitione, πολυπραγμωσύνῃ, injuriisque his illisve illatis hanc indignationem promeruisse, adeoque ipsum D. Spanhemium hujus fortunæ omnisque universim odii esse fabrum. quæ, quo jure quave injuria dicantur non inquiro, hanc litem minimè facturus meam. Sufficiat narraffe quæ dicuntur, quemadmodum & D. Spanhemius in Epistola, facta tantum narrat; atque obfervaffe hujus odii causas non esse controversias illas, quibus D. Spanhemius eas imputatas vellet.
units.tr: The Brethren hate factious pamphlets and academic tumults from the heart, and they shrink from such things more than D. Spanheim perhaps does himself, whom they hope has already learned to despise writings of this kind. They would wish such things avoided all the more because they are born, and serve only, to estrange the wills and minds of the Brethren from one another, which ought to have been united. It is true that Cl. D. Spanheim is ill spoken of by many students. But if anyone asks what the cause of such great anger is, they answer at once, with a stern expression, a grim look and a savage, inhuman and restless temper, that he has earned this indignation through anger, avarice, pride, ambition, meddlesomeness [πολυπραγμοσύνη], and injuries inflicted on this person or that, and that D. Spanheim is the author of this misfortune and of all the hatred in general. By what right or wrong these things are said I do not inquire, since I do not intend to make this quarrel my own. It is enough to have related what is said, as D. Spanheim too says in his Letter that he only relates the facts; and to have observed that the causes of this hatred are not those controversies to which D. Spanheim would wish them imputed.

units.la: In eo D. Spanhemius multus est, ut demonstret dissidia hæc Ecclesiastica in Belgio jam ante annum MDCLXXII. fuisse orta, neque illi Anno originem debere, atque inibi tanquam sycophanta miserè vapulat Gelasius Major, quem id asseruisse conatur Lectori suo persuadere. Verùm, nec Gelasius, nec Timotheus,
units.tr: In this part D. Spanheim labours hard to show that these ecclesiastical dissensions in Belgium arose already before the year 1672, and do not owe their origin to that year. There Gelasius Major, whom he tries to persuade his reader asserted this, is roundly thrashed as a sycophant. But neither Gelasius nor Timothy,

units.la: nec ullus diſctorum Novatorum initium dissidiorum & controversiarum in Belgio exordiuntur ab Anno cIↄ Iↄ CLXXII. Qui de illis quæ post eum annum gesta sunt loquuntur atque inde malorum originem repetunt, non tam ad ipsas controverfias earumque originem, quam ad illas ipsas mirum quantùm multiplicatas, ad furiosas vociferationes ingeminatosque clamores de schismate faciundo, fratribus extrudentis, Hagare pellenda spectant. Istiusmodi consilia, mediaque illuc tendentia ab illo tempore prodierunt, atque aures percusserunt feralia istiusmodi carmina indies magis magisque; nec fine Deo haftenus frustra fuerunt. Nec mirum cuiquam videatur fi ifthoc strepitu excitati sint quam plurimi, pro pace Hierofolymæ & Egregiorum virorum fama vigilaturi.
units.tr: nor any of the new teachers, begins the origin of the disputes and controversies in Belgium from the year 1672. Those who speak of what was done after that year and trace the source of the evils from it look not so much to the controversies themselves and their origin as to those quarrels, multiplied to an astonishing degree, to the furious shouting and repeated clamours about making a schism, thrusting out brethren, and driving out Hagar. Plans of this kind and measures tending that way have come forth since that time, and such dreadful songs have struck the ears more and more every day; nor, up to now, without God's doing, have they been in vain. Nor should it seem strange to anyone if many were roused by this din, who would keep watch for the peace of Jerusalem and the reputation of distinguished men.

units.la: Quæ de Cartefio, Coccejo, Wittichio disserit, Aliorum erit examinare. Gratiæ debentur Spanhemio, quod occasionem Viris doctis dederit veram dissidiorum rixarumque historiam texendi, & quid Coccejo, quid Wittichio, quid Cartefio factum fuerit, quid Callero creatum molestiæ, penitius enodandi atque explicandi, quo occulta & dispersa hactenus quam plurima retegentur.
units.tr: What he says about Descartes, Coccejus and Wittich, others will examine. Thanks are due to Spanheim, because he has given learned men the occasion to weave a true history of the dissensions and quarrels, and to unfold and explain more fully what was done to Coccejus, to Wittich and to Descartes, and what trouble was caused to Callerus, so that the many things hidden and scattered until now may be brought to light.

units.la: Ast, Siccine D. Spanhemi soles amicos? laudas venerandum D. Heydanum, laudas D. Coccejum, laudas D. Wittichium, & dum vis videri laudasse quicquid in eos jactari poterat probri, ipsis infers, atque omnia illa quæ in ipsos ullo unquam tempore dicta fuere, effutis artificiosissimè: quæ autem dici non potuere, callidè fingis, ut invidiam ipsis crees.
units.tr: But is this how you treat your friends, D. Spanheim? You praise the venerable D. Heidanus, you praise D. Coccejus, you praise D. Wittich; and while you want to seem to have praised them, you attach to them whatever reproach could be thrown at them, and you artfully babble out everything that was ever said against them at any time. What could not be said, you cunningly invent, so as to stir up hatred against them.

units.la: Narraturus historiam Decreti Ampliff. DD. Curatorum, quo viginti Articuli proscribebantur, incalescit plus satis D. Spanhemius; & quicquid ipsi fuit virium intendit ad probandum effata summorum virorum huic Decreto occasionem dedisse. quasi vero DD. Curatores istis Defensoribus egerent. Extricavit autem Ven. D. Heydanus hanc materiam tam solidè in doctissimis illis suis Considerationibus, ut ipse Spanhemius nihil habeat quod iis reponere vel audeat vel possit. Argumentis agit Vener. Senex, & non lenociniis verborum. Verùm si quid conjectura assequi potis sim, crediderim Spanhemium ejusque Fratres egerrimè tulisse applausum, quo in Belgio receptum fuit id scriptum, nec ferendo fuisse laudes in Cartesium, Coccejum, & Wittichium collatas. Convictos autem de multo passim plurimoque fructu quem consecutæ sunt illæ Considerationes atque edunt quotidie, suspicor judicasse Spanhemii Fratres, è re sua fore, si Spanhemio auctore vel controversiæ illæ tractarentur, à quo labore D. Spanhemius non immeritò abhorret, vel saltem historia quædam ab omnis generis hominibus legenda, ederetur, quæ multis verborum phaleris decora ea solummodo esset dictura, quæ dictos Novatores urere, eosque in Magnatum odium adducere apta nata essent, adeóque Cartesium, Coccejum, Wittichium atro carbone notandos judicâsse. Tantum conjectura hæc est, fateor. gaudebo tamen, si
units.tr: In narrating the history of the Decree of the Most Distinguished Curators, by which twenty articles were proscribed, D. Spanheim grows heated more than enough, and he directs all his strength to proving that the sayings of the great men gave occasion to this Decree, as if the Curators had acted at the urging of those defenders. But the Venerable D. Heidanus has so solidly disentangled this matter in his most learned Considerations that Spanheim himself has nothing he dares or is able to reply. The venerable old man argues with arguments, not with verbal flattery. But if I may guess at anything, I believe that Spanheim and his brethren took very badly the applause with which that writing was received in Belgium, and could not bear the praises bestowed on Descartes, Coccejus and Wittich. Convinced by the great and daily growing fruit which those Considerations have brought and still bring, I suspect the brethren judged it to their advantage if those controversies were treated under Spanheim's authorship (a labour from which D.
