Spanheim not undeservedly shrinks), or at least that some history was published to be read by all sorts of people, which, adorned with many verbal embellishments, would say only those things apt to burn the said innovators and bring them into the hatred of the great, and so would mark Descartes, Coccejus and Wittich with black charcoal. This is only conjecture, I confess. Still, I shall rejoice if

units.la: hic, ut scholæ loquuntur, non fuerit finis operantis: nemo autem mihi perfuadeat hunc finem hujus operis non esse.
units.tr: this is not, as the schoolmen say, the end of the one working [finis operantis]. No one, however, will persuade me that this is not the aim of this work.

units.la: Qui Historias scribunt ut decet, res gestas quemadmodum gestæ sunt, narrant, nihil de suo addunt, nihil detrahunt vel caute dissimulant, nihil importuna exafperatione vel exosa emollitione invertunt. Sed, præfracte ac jurato quasi contraria omnia agit Spanhemius; nec recte de horum malorum origine, nec recte de caufis, pejus autem de rebus gestis, & peffime de remediis scribit.
units.tr: Those who write histories as they should relate the deeds as they were done; they add nothing of their own, take nothing away or craftily conceal anything, and distort nothing through unseasonable exasperation or hateful softening. But Spanheim proceeds stubbornly, and as if under oath, in everything to the contrary. He writes neither rightly about the origin of these evils, nor rightly about their causes; worse about the deeds done, and very badly about the remedies.

units.la: Veram originem progressumque hujus mali persequatur aliquis, si ab æmulationibus quæ Academias inter Trajectensem ad Rhenum & Lugduno Batavam fuerunt perpetuæ, tanquam fonte derivanda statuerit. Ab ipsis incunabulis in illa diversa prorsus methodo studia instituebant- tur, ac in ista consueverant. Trajectini Ductore Celeberr. D. Voetio præcipuam practicæ theologiæ operam navabant; addiscebatur passim plurimumque lingua Anglicana præ Hebræa & Græca; vertebantur in linguam vernaculam Autores Angli, nectebantur & solvebantur Conscientiæ Casus ; recitabantur Conciones promiscuè, omni remoto delectu ac discrimine, nihil referebat an Episcopales, an Presbyterianos an Independentes haberent Auctores: studia Academica triennî spatio absolvebantur. Tales concionatores in suggestus passim protrudebantur. Consistoria, Classes, Ecclesiæ istiusmodi discipulis replebantur. Æmulatio lites peperit & contentiones fovit. neque illæ intra privatos parietes manserunt. Quæstiones motæ de Coma, Canonicis, Fœnore trapezitico, Sabbato, æque agitatæ non tantum inter Profeffores, sed & inter Pastores Ministros Ecclesiæ, coram populo, in consistoriis, classibus, Synodis, Ampliff. & Nobiliff. DD. Ordinum comitiis. Atque ut non raro fieri consuevit, prout lis litem generat, multiplicatæ contentiones. Auditores præceptorum placitis addictiores magis quam par erat in partes ire, earumque studio segregei facti mutuo vix frui amore, sugillare
units.tr: Someone might trace the true origin and progress of this evil if he decided it must be derived, as from a fountain, from the rivalries which were constant between the Academy at Utrecht on the Rhine and the one at Leiden. From their very cradles, studies were pursued in those places by a method quite different from that of the others. At Utrecht, under the leadership of the very celebrated D. Voetius, they devoted their principal effort to practical theology; English was learned everywhere and far more than Hebrew and Greek; English authors were translated into the vernacular; cases of conscience were tied and untied; sermons were recited indiscriminately, with all selection and distinction set aside, and it made no difference whether the authors were Episcopalians, Presbyterians or Independents; academic studies were completed in the space of three years. Such preachers were thrust into the pulpits everywhere; consistories, classes and congregations were filled with such disciples. Rivalry bred disputes and fostered contentions, and these did not remain within private walls. Questions were raised about wigs, canonries, usury and the Sabbath, and debated not only among the professors but also among the pastors and ministers of the Church, before the people, in consistories, classes, synods, and the assemblies of the Most Distinguished and Noble Lords of the States. And, as often happens when one dispute begets another, the contentions multiplied. The hearers, more attached to their teachers' opinions than was right, went over to the parties, and being divided by their zeal they scarcely enjoyed mutual love, but

units.la: mordere se invicem, quæ placerent his, displicere illis.
units.tr: bit one another, whatever pleased these displeasing those.

units.la: Eos, qui se Trajectinis opponebant habebat illorum temporum Magistratuum favor, quod per Lugdunenfium positiones opinionesque illæsa magis conservari videbatur Authoritas publica. Displicuere Magistratibus mores illorum, qui seu in Synodis votis inferiores, seu cohibiti à Politicâ Majestate in quæstionibus de Canonicis, & fœnore Trapezitico aliisque Rempub. spectantibus, causas illas de suggestu coram plebe non sine applausu, (perperam enim non raro judicat assectibus occupatum vulgus) cum fervore viriumque intensione disceptabant acerrimè: nec tantum de iis quæ inter ipsos essent controversa pro concionibus disceptare, sed & publicum regimen Magistratuumque acta sugillare, factam cum hostibus pacem, pacta cum aliis fœdera indignari publicè non verebantur. Atque hinc postea factum, ut præcipuarum quarundam Urbium in Hollandiâ Magistratus, hoc fidere afflatos Pastores à consistoriis nonnonnunquam nominatos atque electos reprobarint: cujus rei invidiam in immerentes Novatores scil. conferre studei Spanhemius. ast, ipse sibi turdus cacavit malum.
units.tr: Those who opposed the Utrecht men were supported by the favour of the magistrates of those times, because public authority seemed better preserved by the positions and opinions of the Leiden men. The magistrates disliked the manners of those who, either inferior in votes in synods, or restrained by the political majesty from disputing on questions of canonries, usury and other matters touching the commonwealth, argued bitterly, with fervour and every effort of strength, from the pulpit before the crowd, not without applause (for the crowd, occupied with its passions, often judges wrongly). Nor did they only argue from the pulpit about what was controversial among themselves; they were not ashamed to publicly carp at the government and the acts of the magistrates, and to be indignant that peace had been made with enemies and treaties with others. Hence it later came about that the magistrates of some principal towns in Holland, inspired by this spirit, rejected pastors who had sometimes been nominated and elected by the consistories. Spanheim seeks to lay the odium of this matter upon the undeserving innovators; but, as the saying goes, the thrush has fouled its own nest.

units.la: Celebris erat per integrum Belgium pei aliquot annos quaestio de Sabbato, nec leviter animos turbabat; & revera de rebus non de verbis hic disputabatur, agebatui de praecepto Dei, & quidem primae tabulae, neque logomachia illa fuit, sed statu quaestionis rite posito alter asseruit, altei negavit. Narrant, ex Celeberr. Voeti ore feral es has voces haustas fuisse, quaesti haec de Sabbato non poterit nisi per schismc decidi, quae si vera sint, explicata atque ir promptu est origo mali & frustra alib quaeritur hujus calamitatis radix, qua praesto est. Eadem enim forte & hodie Discipulis stat sententia, quae quondam Praeceptori.
units.tr: The question about the Sabbath was for some years famous throughout all Belgium, and it stirred minds not lightly. Indeed, here the dispute concerned things, not words: it was a matter of God's precept, and of the first table of the Law, and it was not a war of words; once the state of the question was properly set, one side asserted and the other denied. They report that from the mouth of the very celebrated Voetius these fatal words were heard: "This question about the Sabbath cannot be settled except by schism." If these words are true, the origin of the evil is explained and lies ready to hand, and the root of this calamity is vainly sought elsewhere when it is at hand. For perhaps even today the opinion of the disciples is the same as once that of the teacher.

units.la: Sed, quare D. Spanhemius de quaestione de Sabbato ortisque pro ea controversiis tam pauca, ut studio videatur de ea tacuisse? Nihil ipsi frequentius, inquies quam ea omnia quæ ipsum non juvant vel instituto ipsius sunt adversa dissimulando negligere. Sic sicco citoque pede quasi scopulos præterveêta ipsius oratio bella inter Celeberr. D. Voetium & Clariss. Marefium Aliosque tacet. Fateor , frequentissimum esse Clariss. Spanhemio præcipuas historiæ partes intactas negligere, sed aliam tamen causam latere suspicor, quare hasce rixas dissimulet. Quantum ad quæstionem de Sabbato , stat à partibus Calvini , cujus sententiam amplexi sunt ii, qui hodiè Novatores audiunt atque ob illam vapulant. Maluit igitur de illa silere, quam ingrata narratione Fratribus suis molestus esse. Idque si præstitisset tacito indicio nec prolocuta consessione patefactum fuisset , exosos Fratres non semper accusari merito suo.
units.tr: But why does Spanheim pass over the controversy about the Sabbath and the disputes that arose over it in such few words, so that he seems to have deliberately kept silent about it? You will say that nothing is more typical of him than to neglect, by glossing over, everything that does not help him or runs against his purpose. And so his oration slips past these quarrels, between the famous Voetius and the distinguished Maresius and others, as if over rocks, with dry feet and at full speed, and says nothing of them. I admit that it is very typical of the illustrious Spanheim to leave the main parts of the history untouched, but I suspect another reason lies behind his keeping these squabbles quiet. On the question of the Sabbath, he sides with Calvin, whose view was embraced by those who are today called Novatores and are beaten for it. He therefore preferred to be silent about it rather than be a nuisance to his brothers with an unwelcome account. And had he managed this without a hint, and had the matter not been brought out into the open by a spoken confession, the brothers who are hated would not always be accused unjustly.

units.la: Dissentientium itaque in gravissima causa nec levi argumento Theologorum animi exacuebantur in bella ; nec mitigabant voluntatum acerbitatem convitia, obtrectationes , injuriæ. hinc odia ; rixæ & tantum non schisma : impedienti-bus bus id publica auctoritate Ordinibus, doctissimisque scriptis calida concitatissimorum hominum consilia confringentibus moderatisque consiliis perniciosis illis conatibus obviam euntibus D. D. Abr. Heydano, Joh. Coccejo, Aliisque, huic etiam calamitati medicinam quandoque facientibus Synodis Hollandiae Australis.
units.tr: So in this most serious matter, and one not of slight importance, the minds of the theologians who disagreed were sharpened for war. Abuse, slander and injuries did not soften the bitterness of their wills; instead they bred hatred, quarrels, and something not far short of schism. The public authority of the Orders checked this, and the most learned writings broke the hot-headed plans of the most violent men, and the moderate counsels of Abraham Heidanus, Johannes Coccejus and others went against those harmful attempts. The Synods of South Holland also at times provided a remedy for this calamity.

units.la: Ast minime ponebantur odia. Latebant quidem illa & quadam ulciscendi difficultate tenebantur, & quae vetustate sedata credidisses, inveterata mitti nec finiri potuerunt. expectabatur tantum occasio & captanda quaedam oportunitas novo impetu atque intensiore vi bellum fumendi. At quae causae motibusque species? miserae quidem illa & flebilis. Traduntur Philosophemata Cartesii, leguntur scripta Coccejji, ad examen revocantur, sunt quam plurimi qui ea putant esse aliquid, magni fiunt à Doctis, volitant illi per ora Virorum. Vera haec quidem; ast errat multumque sallitur qui hinc repetendas calamitatum nostrarum origines & supputanda rixarum semina autumat. Alia majorisque momenti erant non nulla, ob quæ Spanhemius ejusque Fratres dissidebant ab aliis, quos tamen Fratrum loco habuisse debuissent. Libertatem spirabant hi, & servitutem ferre nescii læsuro papaturientium Fratrum jugo colla subtrahebant. hoc crimen est, hinc illæ lachrymæ. Spirabant autem illi tyrannidem, atque huic dominationis spei quum esset litandum, ea ex Magnorum Virorum scriptis collegerunt & corrasèrunt, quæ detorta & mutilata gravissimæ accusationis argumentum & diræ admodum delationis materiam essent suppeditatura. Experturi an Procerum Plebisque animos ad odium accusatorum Fratrum renovare & revocare possent. Hinc de periculosis Novitatibus clamores, hinc de Atheismo, Scepticismo, Socinianismo, Nestorianismo, Pelagianismo, Chiliasmo accusationes; quorum criminum singula, sijus reddat prætor, deportationem reorum, seu Professorum seu Ministrorum Ecclesiæ, mereantur.
units.tr: Yet the hatreds were by no means laid aside. They lay hidden, and were held in check by a certain difficulty of taking revenge; and things that you would have believed were calmed by the passage of time, grown old, could not be sent away or brought to an end. They only waited for an occasion, and for some opportunity to be seized, to take up the war again with fresh assault and greater force. But what were the causes and the pretexts for the movements? Wretched and lamentable ones indeed. The philosophical writings of Descartes were handed round, the writings of Coccejus were read and called into question. There were very many who thought these things were of some worth; they were esteemed highly by learned men, and they fluttered about on the lips of men. These things are true; but he errs greatly and is badly deceived who claims that the origins of our calamities and the seeds of our quarrels are to be traced back to this. Some other matters, of greater weight, were the reasons why Spanheim and his brothers differed from others whom they should nevertheless have regarded as brothers. They breathed freedom, and, unable to bear slavery, they shook off from their necks the yoke of brothers who were eager for power, a yoke that would have hurt them. This is their crime, and hence those tears. But these men breathed tyranny, and since they had to offer up a sacrifice to this hope of domination, they gathered and scraped together from the writings of great men those passages which, twisted and mutilated, would supply the ground for a most grave accusation and the matter for a most dreadful denunciation. They would test whether they could rekindle and revive the hatred of the nobles and the common people against the accused brothers. Hence the outcries about dangerous innovations, hence the accusations of atheism, skepticism, Socinianism, Nestorianism, Pelagianism and Chiliasm; each of these charges, if the magistrate rendered justice, would earn the deportation of the accused, whether professors or ministers of the Church.

units.la: Hoc modo accusati Cartesii Coccejique quondam Auditores, quique eorum
units.tr: In this way the former pupils of Descartes and Coccejus who were accused, and those who held their writings in high esteem,

units.la: scripta magni faciebant, obviam ire accusatoribus, calumniam contundere, criminaque hæc Orthodoxæ omninò Theologiæ & fcripturariæ, atque innoxiæ Philosophiæ illata dissolvere atque eluere, hoc quidem cum successu, ut brevi temporis spatio plerique viri Doćti & Pacifici veritati illustratæ manum dederint & etiamnum dent, ringentibus frustra Spanhemii Fratribus.
units.tr: set themselves against the accusers, refuted the slander, and dissolved and washed away these charges brought against an entirely orthodox theology and Scripture, and against a harmless philosophy. They did this with such success that in a short space of time most learned and peaceable men gave their hand to the illumined truth, and still do so, while the brothers of Spanheim struggled in vain.

units.la: Incenditur interea Patria funestissimo Gallico, Anglicano & Monasteriensi bello, & Terræ motum terribilem, horresco referens experitur Anno cıↄ ıↄ clxxii. ubique tumultus populares, Magistratus pelluntur, alia prorsus Reipub. redit facies. Tandem votis civium omniumque bonorum, Illustrissimum Araufionensium Principem (vivat diu ad gloriam Dei & Ecclesiæ bonum Reipub. decus!) ad dignitates Avorum evećtum optantium, fit fatis. Jaćtant Spanhemii fratres, suum amorem non leve Principis causæ attulisse pondus, stetisse Novatores à partibus Loevesteinianorum. Egregie callidissiméque commentatam fabulam ! sibi Ecclefiam. & Verbi Dei explicationem concreditam existimant viri minimè turbulentam, aliis mandata gubernacula Rerumpublicarum credunt, didicerunt que non esse πολυπραγμονες. Hoc tamen titulo mirum quantum ferocire Spanhemii Fratres. protinus
units.tr: Meanwhile the fatherland was set ablaze by the most deadly French, English and Münster wars, and, I shudder to report it, a terrible earthquake was felt in the year 1672. Everywhere there were popular uprisings, magistrates were overthrown, and the whole face of the commonwealth changed. At last, to the prayers of all the citizens and all good men, the most illustrious Prince of Orange (may he live long, to the glory of God, the good of the Church and the honour of the commonwealth!), who was desiring to be raised to the dignities of his ancestors, was granted his wish. Spanheim's brothers boast that their love for the Prince's cause brought no slight weight, and that the Novatores took the side of the Loevestein men. A well-contrived and most cleverly devised fable! They think that the Church and the explanation of the Word of God have been entrusted to them, men by no means turbulent; that the government of the commonwealths is committed to others; and they have learned not to be busybodies [πολυπραγμονες]. Yet under this title the brothers of Spanheim grow to a remarkable degree of fierceness, and at once

units.la: Una Eurusque Notusque ruunt , creberque procellis
units.tr: Together the East and South winds rush on, and the Africus, thick with storms,

units.la: Africus , & vastos tollunt ad sidera fluctus.
units.tr: and they raise the vast waves up to the stars.

units.la: Prodit Tractatus Maresii de Afflicto statu studii Theologici in Belgio , in linguam Belgicam vertitur , expunctis tamen illis quæ de suis cum aliis Theologis in Belgio controversiis monuerat Maresius , quas & hic D. Spanhemii prudentia intactas voluit. lucem aspicit scriptum belgicum, 't Bewrigt van Coccejaensche en Cartefiaensche Nieuwigheden / admonitio de Novitatibus Coccejanis & Cartefianis ; eristica scripta D. van Rijssen, Disputationes extraordinariæ Hulsii , & quod est hujus farinæ amplius. In his accusantur & traducuntur Coccejus, Wittichius, Academia Lugduno Batava, Profefsores Pastoresque Cocceji Cartefiique meditationibus addiĉtiores, tamquam fanatici, hæretici aut hæresibus affines, quintæ monarchiæ fautores, Ecclesiæ turbones, hostes Illustrissimi Principis. His, multisque precibus, argumentis, fallaciis sollicitantur Procerum animi ad coërcendos Novatores, imò ad pellendam Hagarem tam Theologicam quam Philosophicam incitantur. Eædem criminationes, eadem fulmina & tonitrua eadem convitia audiebantur in Zelandia & alibi, iidem clamores populi aures non sine commotione de suggestu undique feriebant.
units.tr: There appeared Maresius's treatise on the afflicted state of theological study in Belgium, translated into Dutch, though with those passages removed in which Maresius had recorded his controversies with other theologians in Belgium; these too Spanheim's prudence wanted left untouched. There also came into the light a Dutch writing, 'T Bewrigt van Coccejaensche en Cartesiaensche Nieuwigheden, that is, an admonition concerning the Coccejan and Cartesian innovations; the polemical writings of Van Rijssen, the Extraordinary Disputations of Hulsius, and whatever else is of that sort. In these, Coccejus, Wittichius, the Academy of Leiden, and the professors and ministers who were more inclined to the meditations of Coccejus and Descartes are accused and slandered as fanatics, heretics or men akin to heretics, supporters of the fifth monarchy, disturbers of the Church, and enemies of the most illustrious Prince. By these, and by many prayers, arguments and tricks, the minds of the nobles are urged to restrain the Novatores, indeed to drive out Hagar, both theological and philosophical. The same accusations, the same thunderbolts and the same abuse were heard in Zeeland and elsewhere; the same outcries struck the ears of the people from every pulpit, not without disturbance.

units.la: An his visis, talibus perpessis silere potuerunt Viri omnium Ordinum Pacifici, nemini molesti? hoc ne æquum jus- stumque fuisset? loquela potius lapidibus extorta fuisset. Scribunt itaque & illi; sed eo ipso accusantur turbarum, quasi maledictum ab ipsis & non responsum fuisset, criminique ducitur justa defensio.
units.tr: Could the peaceable men of all the Orders keep silent when they had seen and endured such things, and they harmed no one? Would that have been fair and just? Their speech would rather have been wrung out of them with stones. So they too wrote; but for that very act they are accused of stirring up disturbances, as if the slander had come from them and not an answer, and their just defence is counted as a crime.

units.la: Hæc omnia vix primoribus digitis attingit Spanhemius. Machinas à classe Goesana contra Wittichium adhibitas quibus non artibus conatur excusare? Ast quis in illorum gestis conspiciatur ordo? quid justi? quod vel minum charitatis vel studii veritatis vestigium? Clasficaliter condemnant inauditum, atque insonti stigma novitatis atque αἱρεσοδοξίας inurunt. Caeteras Zelandiae Classes in quibus plurimi Trajectina methodo imbuti latebant, per literas idem ut audeant hortantur. Ad caeteras Belgii Synodos, quibuscum nihil aliàs ipsis Correspondentiae, (sit venia verbo) epistolas quibus & illae in D. Wittichium instigarentur, decernunt, & vix ab Ordinibus Zelandiae hoc in molimine cohibentur, & à Timotheo Verino, succumbente D. Barenzonio frustra de sententia Cl. Wittichii admonentur. Transfalanos nihilominus privatâ ad privatum epistola eo usque adduxerunt & permoverunt, ut Transfilanae Synodi Actis, Classis Goesanae acta insererentur. Hinc nova molimina. Proximo ab isthoc anno Synodus Hollandiae Borealis Woerdam cogenda erat. Correspondens Tranfisalanus quid in Tranfisalana Synodo actum esset narrare atque eandem in Hollandiæ Synodo controversiam movere conatur. Nobilis. Ordinum ad Synodum Deputatus non ignarus qua arte illa omnia gererentur, certusque turbas quæri, publicam auctoritatem huic audaciæ interponens, Correspondenti silentium imperavit, finemque omni de hoc negotio deliberationi fecit. Adeoque inibi hi doli, hæ machinæ atque præstigiæ nihil ipsis profuerunt, atque sunt Nobilis. D.Deputato ab Amplis. & Nobilis. DD. Ordinibus Hollandiæ hoc nomine gratiæ, atque ipsi Tranfisalani Fratres postea ab inceptis destiterunt. Quid erubescis D. Spanhemi? an non hæc digna erant quæ Amico narrarentur? Sed exsequamur cœptum propositi ordinem.
units.tr: Spanheim barely touches on all these matters with the tips of his fingers. What tricks does he try to excuse, the machinations used by the Classis of Goes against Wittichius? But what order is to be seen in their doings? What justice? What trace of even the least charity or zeal for truth? They condemn without a hearing, and brand the innocent man with the stigma of innovation and heresy-opinion [αἱρεσοδοξίας]. They urge the other Classes of Zeeland, in which many who had been steeped in the Utrecht method lay hidden, to dare the same thing by letter. They decree letters to the other Synods of Belgium, with which they had otherwise no correspondence (let me use the word with pardon), by which those too might be stirred up against Wittichius; and they were scarcely restrained in this enterprise by the Orders of Zeeland, and were warned in vain about the opinion of the distinguished Wittichius by Timotheus Verinus, while Barentsen gave way. Nevertheless they brought the men of Utrecht, by private letter to private persons, to such a point and so moved them that the acts of the Classis of Goes were inserted into the acts of the Synod of Utrecht. Hence new contrivances. In the year just past the Synod of North Holland had to be held at Woerden. The correspondent from Utrecht tried to relate what had been done in the Synod of Utrecht and to stir up the same controversy in the Synod of Holland. The noble deputy of the Orders to the Synod, not unaware of the art by which all this was managed, and certain that disturbances were being sought, interposed public authority against this audacity, imposed silence on the correspondent, and brought every deliberation on this business to an end. And so these deceits, these machinations and these juggleries did them no good there, and the noble deputy received thanks for this from the most distinguished and noble Orders of Holland, and the brothers of Utrecht themselves afterwards desisted from their undertakings. Why do you blush, Spanheim? Were these things not worth relating to a friend? But let us follow the order of our plan as we began it.

units.la: Tacet quibus artibus decretum Enchusanæ Synodi Anno cIↄ Iↄ clxxii. Fratres Spanhemii impetrarint. Gelasius hanc prout gesta est, narrat historiam. Tu tamen D. Spanhemi, qui illum legisti gifti illorum afpeƈtu obmutescis.
units.tr: Gelasius tells the story of how the decree of the Enkhuizen Synod of 1672 was obtained by the Spanheim brothers, but he does not say by what tricks. You, Spanheim, who have read his account, fall silent when you see those people's faces.

units.la: Tacet nobiles illos decem Articulos in Edamenfi Synodo ab ipsius Fratribus cusos, plerosque tam crudos, ut ipsæ Borealis Hollandiæ Classes in sequenti Alcmariana Synodo, eos emendare atque emollire necessum putaverint. Obtrudebantur scil. illi articuli ut via pacis, atque ut tales à Classibus in Australi Hollandia tandem fuere receptæ.
units.tr: You say nothing about the ten articles that the brothers forced through the Synod of Edam. Most of them were so crude that the Classes of North Holland themselves thought it necessary to correct and soften them at the following Synod of Alkmaar. The articles were pushed through as a way to peace, and in that form the Classes of South Holland finally accepted them.

units.la: Videbatur itaque in illa Hollandiæ parte res composita, restabant Australis Hollandiæ Classes undecim: ad quas per ordinarios Synodi Deputatos Auctoritate publica decem illi articuli mittuntur eo fine, ut omnia singularum Classium membra illos examinarent atque expenderent, &, si salvâ fide & conscientiâ illæsâ fieri posset, pacis gratia eos amplectèrentur, quò sic pari passu incederent cum Fratribus Hollandiæ Borealis Ecclesiarum Ministris.
units.tr: So the matter seemed settled in that part of Holland, and eleven Classes of South Holland remained. The ten articles were sent to them by the ordinary deputies of the Synod, with public authority, so that every member of each Class might examine and weigh them and, if it could be done with faith kept and conscience unharmed, embrace them for the sake of peace. In this way they would advance on equal terms with the ministers of the churches of North Holland.

units.la: Summa votorum Classium Australis Hollandiæ ad Synodum Leerdamensem delatorum Anno cıↄ ıↄ cıxxv. hæc fuit. Amplecti fe pacis promovendæ ergo decem illos articulos, stipulatâ tamen de non adducendis impofterum fratribus ὁμοψήφοις in suspicionem ἐιρεσδοξίας quadam lege. Quæ & stipulatio in clausulæ modum declarationi Classium subnectebatur, Actisque Synodi inserebatur Legis instar habenda. Neque tamen huc usque à Synodis Borealis Hollandiæ (licet tantum sex in ea sint Classes) impetrari potuit, ut & inibi clausula hæc reciperetur: salvâ tamen pace cum Austrialis Hollandiæ Synodo, Ut ex actis Borealis Hollandiæ Synodi, Anno cIↄ Iↄ cLxxv. & cIↄ Iↄ cLxxvi. liquet.
units.tr: The sum of the votes of the Classes of South Holland, brought to the Synod of Leerdam in 1675, was this: they embraced the ten articles for the sake of promoting peace, but on the condition of a certain stipulated rule that their like-minded brothers [ὁμοψήφοις] should not be brought in future under suspicion of heterodoxy [ἑτεροδοξίας]. This stipulation was appended to the declaration of the Classes in the form of a clause and entered in the acts of the Synod, to be held as a law. Yet up to now the Synods of North Holland (though there are only six Classes there) have not been able to obtain that this clause be accepted there too, "saving however peace with the Synod of South Holland," as is clear from the acts of the Synod of North Holland for 1675 and 1676.

units.la: In Dordracena Synodo Anni cIↄ Iↄ cLxxvi. eadem pacis formula fuit repetita, confirmata, Classibusque intensissimè commendata.
units.tr: In the Synod of Dort of 1676 the same formula of peace was repeated, confirmed, and strongly commended to the Classes.

units.la: Consentiunt itaque Australis Hollandiæ Classes in vias pacis, declarant se nullos Pastores ex suis nosse, qui Novatores audire mereantur, afferunt confirmantque se formulis consensus adhærere ftrictissimè, neminemque nosse qui ab
units.tr: Thus the Classes of South Holland agree to the ways of peace. They declare that they know of no ministers among their own who deserve to hear the Innovators. They affirm and confirm that they hold most strictly to the formulas of consensus, and they know of no one

units.la: illis difcedat. Jubent pacem coli, charitatique ftudere omnes volunt: vetant ullum novationis convitium fieri illis, qui formulis confenfus adhærent. Sic ibi transactum hactenus pacificè.
units.tr: who departs from them. They order that peace be cultivated, and they want all to strive for charity. They forbid any reproach of innovation to be cast at those who hold to the formulas of consensus. So far the matter has been peacefully settled there.

units.la: Quantum ab his diverfi funt Spanhemius ejufque Fratres ? Claffes Auftralis Hollandiæ negant inter ipfos effe qui ab orthodoxia deficiant. Fratres Spanhemii vociferantur plures inter ipfos effe αἱρεδοξʒς perniciofæ doctrinæ reos. Claffes Novatores ignorant talefque in illa Hollandiæ parte reperiri negant, nomen autem Novatorum ut contumeliofum exulare jubent; Fratres vero Spanhemii indies magis magifque & quafi revocatis viribus in accufationem Fratrum coëunt, eofque novitatis reos agunt. Claffes declarant nullum fuorum membrorum à formulis confenfus receffiffe iifve nuntium miffe; Spanhemius omnes has affertiones & obteftationes nihili facit, atque odiofa nec non infolenti hac cum Remonftrantium geftis comparatione perfidiæ & hypocrifeos fufpicionem in fratres jacere non erubescit. Classes ad pacem cohortantur; eam habent, colunt; Spanhemii Fratres bella crepant, lites rixasque exaggerant. Classes tolerantiam Fratribus commendant in illis quae necdum in formulis consensus sunt determinata, qualis certe laude nunquam caruit; Spanhemius unicum silentii remedium praescribit, & quidem tale, quod solis Spanhemii Antagonistis esset imponendum. Egregiam quidem pacis legem! silere ut velis ubi Deus loquitur & te loqui jubet, idque in gratiam contradicentium. Hanc certe si potuissent conditionem amplecti qui Novatores audiunt, non fuisset disputatum tam diu.
units.tr: How different are Spanheim and his brothers! The Classes of South Holland deny that there are among them any who fall away from orthodoxy. The Spanheim brothers cry out that many among them are guilty of heterodox [ἑτερόδοξοι] and pernicious doctrine. The Classes do not know of such men and deny that any are found in that part of Holland, and they order the name of Innovators, as an insult, to be banished. But the Spanheim brothers gather day by day, with their strength as it were renewed, into an accusation of the brothers, and they charge them with novelty. The Classes declare that none of their members has departed from the formulas of consensus or sent word of having done so. Spanheim thinks nothing of all these assertions and protestations, and by an odious comparison, not in keeping with the conduct of the Remonstrants, he is not ashamed to cast on the brothers the suspicion of treachery and hypocrisy. The Classes urge peace; they have it and cherish it. The Spanheim brothers make a noise of war and magnify quarrels and brawls. The Classes commend tolerance to the brothers in those matters which are not yet determined in the formulas of consensus, a praise that has certainly never been lacking to them. Spanheim prescribes one remedy only, silence, and indeed one that ought to be imposed on Spanheim's opponents alone. What an excellent law of peace! You are to be silent, you who wish it, where God speaks and bids you speak, and that for the sake of those who contradict. Certainly, if those who hear the Innovators could have accepted this condition, the dispute would not have lasted so long.

units.la: Optas pacem Spanhemi, concordiam commendas, monumentum posteritati fieri vis τῆς τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὁμονοίας, nec hoc quidem male. Sed, habuissemus pacem, nisi D. Hulsius quietem expulisset: imo habemus pacem, si Fratres tui Decretis Synodorum Leerdamensis & Dordracenae parere velint; nos illas pacis leges amplectimur, probamus, sequimur, reveremur.
units.tr: You long for peace, Spanheim; you commend concord; you want a monument to be made for posterity of the concord of the brothers [τῆς τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὁμονοίας]. That is not a bad wish. But we would have had peace, had not Mr. Hulsius driven out quiet. Indeed we have peace, if your brothers are willing to obey the decrees of the Synods of Leerdam and Dort. We embrace those laws of peace, we approve them, we follow them, and we revere them.

units.la: Quid ni idem faciunt Fratres Tui, quid ni definis res nefarias de Fratribus pessimè suspicari? hoc præsta id faciant Illi eritque lis omnis composita, jungemus dexteras, mutuoque fruemur amore.
units.tr: Why do your brothers not do the same? Why do you not cease to hold such wicked suspicions of the brothers? Do this, and let them do the same: all strife will be settled, we shall join right hands, and we shall enjoy mutual love.

units.la: Ast, hæc omnia, quasi facta non essent, Spanhemi, dissimulas. hæccine prisca fides est, & simplicitas Tanto Theologo digna?
units.tr: But you dissemble all this, Spanheim, as if it had never happened. Is this the ancient faith and the simplicity worthy of so great a theologian?

units.la: Refert porro, quid Helvetii, quid Germani, quid Galli, quid Doćti quidam viri judicaverint de Theologia D. Cocceji, quid de Philosophia Cartefii statuerint. Verùm, quid hæc omnia ad rem faciunt? nos rationem reddituri non sumus ejus, quid docuerimus ex hujus vel illius sententia, probatum ab hoc rejećtum ab illo: sed, quid ex Verbo Dei servata bona conscientia tradiderimus Auditoribus nostris. Ponamus, Omnes ubique & Academias & Eruditos se Coccejo & Cartefio opposuisse, atque ab iis omnes Virorum horum meditationes damnatas, an inde concludere erit Theologiam hanc & Philosophiam esse falsam, erroneam & periculofam? neutiquam. hoc enim si procederet argumentum, pari ratione Reformationem per Lutherum, Calvinum & alios factam optimo jure refutasse dicendi forent Pontificii, ut nos Sleydani aliorumque historiae docent. Totus mundus oppositum se Euangelio. nec definit eo Euangelium esse ipsissimum Verbum Dei. Non comparo Cocceji Meditationes vel Cartesii cogitata, Verba hominum, cum Euangelio, quod foret impium. absit hoc! sed invicto argumento demonstro, tales relationes comparationesve nullum posse creare praejudicium optimae causae.
units.tr: Further, he reports what the Swiss, the Germans, the French, and certain learned men have judged of the theology of Mr. Cocceius, and what they have decided about the philosophy of Descartes. But what has all this to do with the matter? We are not going to render an account of what we have taught on the judgment of this man or that, approved by one and rejected by another; but of what we have handed on to our hearers from the Word of God, keeping a good conscience. Suppose that everywhere both academies and learned men have opposed Cocceius and Descartes, and that all the meditations of these men have been condemned by them: will it follow that this theology and this philosophy are false, erroneous, and dangerous? By no means. For if this argument held, the Papists would rightly be able to say, by the same reasoning, that they had refuted the Reformation carried out by Luther, Calvin, and others, as the histories of Sleidan and others teach us. The whole world opposed the Gospel, and yet the Gospel is not for that reason ceased to be the very Word of God. I do not compare the meditations of Cocceius or the thoughts of Descartes, mere words of men, with the Gospel, for that would be impious. Far from it! But I show by an unanswerable argument that such reports and comparisons can create no prejudice against a good cause.

units.la: Praeterea, narrat quaedam quae facta sunt & proflant publice, sed non narrat, quibus prensationibus, epistolis, artificiis impetrata sint, quae recensent decreta. sed & narrat quae nunquam facta sunt. pag. 99. narrat causas & rationes D. Wittichii cum Geldris, Ultrajectinis, Zelandis, Transfsalanis, Frisiis. Cum Geldris disputare necessum habuit de motu terrae, iisque satisfecit, ut testantur acta publica. nihil igitur est, cur haec recenseri hic debuerint, nisi id necessum fuerit ad augendam invidiam. Quid Tranfifalani egerint dictum superiùs est, certè eos ipsorum spes est frustrata. Insula Goefana omnem Zelandiam non absolvit. De Ultrajectinis & Frifiis nihil in Actis reperitur.
units.tr: Besides, he narrates some things that were done and are publicly known, but he does not narrate by what solicitations, letters, and devices the decrees he recounts were obtained. He also narrates things that were never done. On page 99 he narrates the causes and reasons of Mr. Wittichius with the people of Gelderland, Utrecht, Zeeland, Groningen, and Friesland. He had to dispute with the people of Gelderland about the motion of the earth, and he satisfied them, as the public acts attest. There is therefore no reason why these things should be recounted here, unless it were necessary in order to increase odium. What the people of Groningen did has been said above; certainly their hope has been frustrated. The island of Goeree does not absolve all of Zeeland. Nothing is found in the Acts about the people of Utrecht or Friesland.

units.la: Narrat & quæ ante aliquot annos in Helvetia acta sunt. Sed non narrat, mutatam jam ibi prorsus rerum faciem. Plerosque in Helvetia & Reformatis Germaniæ Academiis Profeffores Meditationes Cocceji & Philofophemata Cartefii maximi facere. Itaque refert non quæ jam fiunt, sed quæ facta sunt & fuerunt, adeoque dissimulat quæ ipsum non juvant, hâc opinor fiduciâ, paucissimis quænam in Helvetia hodiè doceantur, innotuisse, id-que plurimos latere. Epistolas familiares Theologorum citat. Quid autem juvat prodere secreta? optimo consilio tacet quomodo aliquando epistolam Clariff. D. Heydano inscriptam alteri ad ipsum missæ inclusam, non dicam reseraverit avidus cognoscendi quid in ea scriptum effet. nam id casui imputari posset, sed reseratam legerit, quædam de ipso scripta subductis lineis conspicua præ cæteris esse voluerit, reseratamque & hunc in modum illustratam Ven. D. Heydano tradere aulus fuerit. Quo nomine ipsi gratias actas nemo crediderit.
units.tr: He also narrates what was done some years ago in Switzerland. But he does not narrate that the face of things there has now been wholly changed. Most professors in Switzerland and in the Reformed academies of Germany hold the Meditations of Cocceius and the philosophical doctrines of Descartes in the highest esteem. So he reports not what is now being done, but what was done and what was the case in the past, and so he conceals what does not help him, I suppose in the confidence that very few people know what is taught in Switzerland today, and that most are ignorant of it. He cites the familiar letters of theologians. But what good does it do to betray secrets? With the best discretion he is silent about how, once, eager to know what was written in it, he did not, I will not say open, but read a letter addressed to the most distinguished Mr. Heidanus, enclosed with another sent to him, and having opened it, he wanted certain things written about himself to stand out more than others by marks drawn beneath them; and having thus opened and illustrated it, he dared to hand it to the venerable Mr. Heidanus. No one would believe that thanks were given to him for this.

units.la: Atque hæc quidem hactenus sufficiat observasse. Clarum erit ex illis minimùm, quod
units.tr: Let it suffice to have observed these things thus far. From these at least it will be clear

units.la: Nil dignum tanto tulit hic promissor hiatu.
units.tr: This promiser brought forth nothing worthy of so great a gaping.

units.la: Plura procul dubio dabunt illi quibus coram insultat. Apage sermonum flores & verborum lenocinia aculeos tegentia. hebetantur illis oculi, & lumini obducuntur tenebræ, atque ad hoc sunt unicè comparata. Quanto melius autem nobiscum ageretur, si non foret necessum in tali scriptorum genere occupari! Utinam homines illi quæ restinguendo huic incendio facere apta nata sunt, depositis odiis afferrent? Oremus autem Deum ut domet corda ipsorum, servet Ecclesiam, reddatque Hierosolymæ pacem!
units.tr: No doubt those to whom he insults face to face will give more. Away with flowers of speech and the cajolery of words that hide stings! Their eyes are dulled by these, and darkness is cast over the light, and for this purpose alone they are fitted. How much better it would be for us if we were not obliged to be occupied with this kind of writing! Would that those men would lay aside their hatreds and bring what they were born fit to do to quench this fire! But we pray God to tame their hearts, to preserve the Church, and to restore peace to Jerusalem!
